psychology.executiveSummary: The vision is fundamentally sound but contains a specific, well-documented failure mode that will kill the fun if not designed against deliberately. The good news: the user has correctly diagnosed the disease. "Make a bunch of troops, attack/defend, repeat" is shallow not because it lacks systems, but because it lacks MEANINGFUL DIFFERENTIATED DECISIONS — every game collapses to the same dominant line (mass the best unit, A-move). Sid Meier's definition is the scalpel here: a game is "a series of interesting decisions," and a decision is only interesting when no option is clearly dominant, the options aren't equal, and the player can make an informed choice. The current loop fails all three. Adding diplomacy, research, and a real-resource economy is the RIGHT instinct because each is a potential source of interesting decisions — BUT the same additions are the single biggest risk to the vision. The user's own reference points (Stellaris, Civilization) are the textbook cautionary tales: in real-time, layered subsystems do not automatically deepen play; past a threshold they produce cognitive overload, analysis paralysis, and late-game micromanagement tedium — the exact opposite of the "fast, engaging, envelops you in complexity" goal. The decisive principle, supported across the literature, is DEPTH WITHOUT COMPLEXITY ("elegant" systems): few rules, many emergent consequences. The failure mode is COMPLEXITY WITHOUT DEPTH: many rules, few real choices, lots of clicking. The whole project lives or dies on which side of that line each new system lands. My recommendation is to treat "fun" as an engineering constraint — adopt a small number of hard design rules (decision budget per minute, no-dominant-strategy test, automate-the-tedium, progressive disclosure) and prototype the strategic layer in YAML/Lua FAST before committing to the expensive 32-facing sprite art, because the art cost ceiling means a wrong systemic bet is very expensive to unwind.
keyFindings: WHY RTS IS FUN (the target to preserve): Fun in games is the brain's reward for mastering patterns (Koster's Theory of Fun) — games are 'learning machines,' and they go boring the instant the pattern is mastered and nothing new is left to learn. RTS sustains this via DECISION DENSITY: at any moment you are juggling economy vs army, expansion vs defense, tech timing, and positioning under time pressure. StarCraft 2 is the benchmark precisely because its asymmetric races force constant macro-vs-micro tension — 'a player with perfect macro and no micro beats great micro and bad macro every time.' That continuous, non-trivial trade-off under a clock is the engine of flow.

PRECISE DIAGNOSIS of 'troops, attack/defend, repeat': It is not too SIMPLE — it is too SOLVED. The loop offers low decision density and a dominant strategy (build the cost-efficient unit, mass it, A-move). By Meier's test it fails on all counts: one option is clearly best (not interesting), unit choices are near-equivalent reskins (no meaningful differentiation), and there's little hidden information to reward judgment. The symptom in big-army RTS/4X is the DEATHBALL/DOOMSTACK: when all units share one purpose and a single blob is strictly optimal, skill expression collapses to 'who has the bigger ball.' This is a lack of meaningful, differentiated choices and high skill expression — exactly what the user named.

FLOW IS THE REAL-TIME CONSTRAINT (Csikszentmihalyi): fun lives in the narrow channel where challenge ≈ skill. Too much challenge/complexity per second → ANXIETY (and in a real-time game, panic and paralysis); too little → BOREDOM. This is the crux of the vision's tension: 4X-depth raises the challenge axis, but in REAL TIME the player can't pause to absorb it, so the same systems that read as 'deep' in turn-based Civ read as 'overwhelming' or 'unmanageable' in real time. Stellaris/Paradox players literally describe choosing 'between tedium and inefficiency' — flow broken in both directions at once.

THE DEPTH-vs-COMPLEXITY DISTINCTION is the single most important design lever, and it is NOT the same axis. COMPLEXITY = number of rules/systems/inputs the player must track (cognitive cost). DEPTH = number of meaningfully different viable strategies that emerge (decision payoff). ELEGANT design (e.g. Pax Pamir, Go, chess) maximizes depth-per-unit-complexity: simple actions, opaque/rich strategy, 'easy to learn, hard to master.' The vision's danger is adding complexity (more subsystems, more menus) and assuming depth follows. It often doesn't — you can add a whole diplomacy screen and create zero new interesting decisions if the optimal diplomatic play is always the same.

WHERE ADDED SYSTEMS DEEPEN vs DESTROY: Research/diplomacy/economy deepen play ONLY when they (a) create new trade-offs against the core loop (e.g. teching costs army NOW), (b) interact with each other and with combat (cross-system dynamics), and (c) have no dominant default. They DESTROY play when they are parallel busywork — independent meters you optimize on autopilot, or micromanagement that scales with empire size (Stellaris' '100 planets = mindless clicking'). The 4X 'boring endgame' is structural: interfaces tuned for the early game collapse under late-game numbers where each decision matters less but costs the same time. A real-time game amplifies this brutally.

MDA / SCHELL framing for the team: design from MECHANICS (rules) but VALIDATE at AESTHETICS (the felt experience). The user's goals — 'engaging,' 'envelops you in complexity,' 'meaningful decisions' — are aesthetic targets (Challenge, Discovery, Expression, Fellowship via diplomacy). The job is to find the minimal mechanics whose DYNAMICS produce those feelings, and ruthlessly cut mechanics that don't. Schell's Lens of Meaningful Choices: count the real choices, check none is dominant, check the player understands the stakes. If a system fails that lens, it's decoration, not design.

PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE is the proven antidote to the onboarding/overload problem: reveal complexity in layers as the player demonstrates mastery, not all at once. This is how you reconcile 'fast and accessible' with 'deep and complex' — Civ does it with eras/advisors; the flow literature calls it scaffolding (difficulty rising with skill). Without it, a 4X-deep RTS dumps its full system surface on minute one and pushes new players out of flow into anxiety, and bores experts who must wade through tutorials.

ENGINE REALITY is favorable but the ART CEILING is the real constraint on iteration. Confirmed in-repo: support-power system (OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/SupportPowers/), an Encyclopedia widget (OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/Encyclopedia.cs + Widgets/Logic/EncyclopediaLogic.cs), diplomacy/stances, prerequisites/tech-tree, veterancy, Lua scripting. So the strategic LAYER is cheap to prototype in YAML/Lua. But every new differentiated unit needs 32-facing sprite art — meaning a wrong systemic bet is expensive to walk back. This argues for proving the fun of the strategic systems with placeholder/recolored art BEFORE funding the art pipeline.
recommendations: ADOPT A 'DECISION BUDGET,' NOT A 'FEATURE BUDGET.' Define a target decision density (e.g. the player should face ~1 genuinely interesting, non-trivial choice every 10-20 seconds, and near-zero forced busywork clicks). Every proposed system must justify itself by ADDING interesting decisions per minute, not features. If diplomacy adds a screen but the optimal play is always the same, it spends complexity and buys no depth — cut or redesign it. This operationalizes Meier directly.

APPLY THE NO-DOMINANT-STRATEGY TEST to every faction, unit, and system. For each country's unique unit/building, write down: 'what does this make me do differently, and when is it the WRONG choice?' If a unit has no situation where you'd skip it, it's a stat-stick, not a strategy. Differentiate factions by STRATEGIC USE (the user's exact word) — e.g. one country excels at fast raiding economies, another at fortified defense, another at tech-rush — so the matchup itself, not unit stats, generates the interesting decisions (this is StarCraft 2's asymmetry lesson). Aim for soft rock-paper-scissors at the COMPOSITION level so the deathball is never strictly optimal.

KILL THE DEATHBALL BY DESIGN. Use the documented counters: (a) give high-tier units real vulnerabilities so they must be screened by cheaper units (forces composition, not blobbing); (b) make territory/objectives matter so splitting forces is rewarded (Company of Heroes' territory-for-resources model eliminates harvester micro AND forces map-wide decisions simultaneously — a two-birds design worth stealing); (c) make a pure top-tier stack cost-inefficient vs a mixed force. Positioning and combined arms, not click-speed, should be the skill axis — this also keeps it 'retro' without becoming an APM grind.

BUDGET COMPLEXITY BY MAKING SYSTEMS INTERACT, NOT MULTIPLY. The difference between Civ-depth and Stellaris-tedium is whether subsystems CROSS-COUPLE or run in parallel. Three systems that feed each other (economy gates research, research unlocks diplomacy leverage, diplomacy reshapes the map you fight over) create combinatorial depth from few rules — elegant. Five independent meters each optimized on autopilot create complexity with no depth — tedious. Prefer FEWER systems with RICHER interactions. This is the single highest-leverage rule for hitting 'enveloping complexity' without grand-strategy slowness.

AUTOMATE THE TEDIUM, SURFACE THE DECISION. The Stellaris lesson is explicit: never make the player choose between tedium and inefficiency. Anything that scales with empire size and has an obviously-correct answer (resource hauling, repeat production, base micro) should be automatable WITHOUT a competitive penalty, so the player's attention stays on the interesting decisions. OpenRA already removes some of this; lean into it. The test: if a task is mandatory, repetitive, and has a known-best answer, it's busywork — automate it or cut it.

USE PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE AND THE EXISTING ENCYCLOPEDIA AS A FLOW TOOL, NOT JUST A CODEX. Layer the systems: early game exposes the core RTS loop; research/diplomacy/strategic-resources unlock and reveal their UI as the match (or the player's account-level mastery) progresses. Tie the real-ore CODEX into this — surface a resource's strategic role exactly when it first becomes relevant, turning lore into a just-in-time tutorial. This keeps the challenge-skill curve inside the flow channel (Csikszentmihalyi) and prevents minute-one overload. The Encyclopedia widget already exists to host it.

PROTOTYPE THE STRATEGIC LAYER IN YAML/LUA WITH PLACEHOLDER ART BEFORE COMMITTING SPRITES. Because 32-facing art is the cost ceiling, prove the FUN of factions/research/diplomacy/resources first using recolored existing units and the existing trait/prerequisite/support-power/Lua systems. Run the no-dominant-strategy and decision-density tests in real playtests. Only commission bespoke art for units whose strategic role has already proven to generate interesting decisions. This sequences the cheap-to-change (systems) before the expensive-to-change (art).

PLAYTEST FOR THE AESTHETIC, MEASURE THE DYNAMIC (MDA in practice). 'Is it fun?' is not measurable; proxies are. Track: how often the same opening/composition wins (dominant-strategy alarm), how long players sit idle or stare at menus (analysis-paralysis/flow-break alarm), late-game actions-per-minute spent on busywork vs decisions (tedium alarm), and whether new players reach a first win without rage-quitting (onboarding/flow alarm). Let these metrics gate which systems ship — fun by construction, not by hope.
risks: ANALYSIS PARALYSIS IN REAL TIME (highest risk). Civ-style depth assumes the player can stop and think; an RTS clock does not allow it. If per-second decision load exceeds what a player can process, the result is not 'deep' — it's panic, freezing, or tuning out. Stellaris/CK players paper over this WITH PAUSE; the user explicitly does NOT want grand-strategy slowness. You cannot import 4X breadth wholesale into real time and keep it fast. Mitigation: hard decision-density ceilings, automation, and disclosure — and accept that some Civ systems simply won't survive the translation.

COMPLEXITY MASQUERADING AS DEPTH. The most likely way this fails is shipping many systems that each look strategic but collapse to a dominant line, producing more UI and clicking but no new interesting decisions. The player feels busy, not engaged — the 'troops/attack/repeat' problem returns wearing a diplomacy hat. Mitigation: the no-dominant-strategy lens applied per-system, mercilessly.

LATE-GAME TEDIUM / SNOWBALL. 4X economies snowball and their micromanagement scales with size while each decision's marginal weight shrinks — the documented '4X boring endgame.' In real time this becomes unmanageable clicking, not strategy. Mitigation: cap or abstract scaling, automate size-scaling tasks, and design matches to resolve before the tedium threshold (shorter strategic arcs than a 4X campaign).

FACTION FANTASY vs BALANCE TENSION. 'Real countries reflecting real military tech' invites realism-driven imbalance (some real arsenals are just better) and the trap of cosmetic-only uniques (a reskinned tank is not a unique strategy). Mitigation: differentiate by STRATEGIC ROLE and asymmetric playstyle (StarCraft model), balance for the matchup not the spec sheet, and accept deliberate departures from realism where realism would create a dominant faction.

ONBOARDING CLIFF / AUDIENCE SPLIT. A 4X-deep RTS risks being too much for RTS players and too fast for 4X players, landing in an empty middle. Without strong progressive disclosure, the full system surface on minute one pushes newcomers into anxiety and churn. Mitigation: layered reveal, strong tutorialization via the Codex, and a genuinely simple core loop that is fun BEFORE any advanced system is unlocked.

ART COST LOCK-IN. The 32-facing sprite requirement means systemic bets get frozen into expensive assets early; discovering post-art that a unit/faction isn't fun is costly to reverse. Mitigation: prove systems with placeholder art first (see recommendations); treat art commissioning as a downstream commitment gated by proven fun.

SCOPE / SOLO-FEASIBILITY. This is effectively a new game on an existing engine: new factions, new art, new strategic layer, new balance pass, new onboarding. The realistic failure is not bad design but unfinished design. Mitigation: ship the smallest version that proves the thesis — e.g. 3-4 sharply differentiated factions and ONE new cross-coupled strategic system done well — before broadening.

precedents.name: StarCraft 2 (asymmetric RTS benchmark)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Three races that play completely differently (not stat reskins), balanced against each other, with constant macro-vs-micro tension forcing trade-offs every few seconds. Differentiation is by playstyle/strategic identity, not raw numbers.
precedents.outcome: The genre's gold standard for competitive depth and longevity; widely cited as 'never replicated' for its decision density and skill ceiling.
precedents.lessonForUs: Differentiate the user's real-country factions by STRATEGIC USE and asymmetric playstyle, not unit stats. The interesting decisions should emerge from the matchup and from juggling economy/army/tech under a clock — that is the proven fun engine to preserve while modernizing the look.

precedents.name: Stellaris / Paradox grand strategy (the cautionary tale the user cited)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Layered many parallel subsystems (pops, economy, diplomacy, research) that scale with empire size; relied on pause and sector automation to cope.
precedents.outcome: Acclaimed early game, but widely criticized late-game tedium: players forced to choose 'between tedium and inefficiency,' 100-planet management becomes 'mindless clicking,' flow broken in both directions.
precedents.lessonForUs: This is exactly what NOT to import into real time. Adding subsystems does not equal depth; parallel, size-scaling micromanagement is the failure mode. Cross-couple a FEW systems instead, automate size-scaling busywork, and keep match length under the tedium threshold.

precedents.name: Company of Heroes (territory-for-resources RTS)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Replaced harvester micromanagement with TERRITORY CONTROL for resources, and emphasized cover/flanking/positioning over click-speed and unit spam.
precedents.outcome: Celebrated as the RTS that delivers strategic depth with far less micromanagement; positioning-driven rather than APM-driven.
precedents.lessonForUs: A single mechanic (territory = economy) simultaneously removes tedious harvester micro, forces map-wide strategic decisions, and discourages the deathball by rewarding spread/forward presence. High depth-per-complexity — exactly the elegant pattern to emulate.

precedents.name: Civilization series (interesting decisions + progressive disclosure)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Built on Meier's 'series of interesting decisions' doctrine; manages enormous system breadth via eras, advisors, and layered reveal so complexity arrives gradually.
precedents.outcome: Decades-long 'one more turn' engagement; the canonical example of deep-but-learnable strategy.
precedents.lessonForUs: Two lessons: (1) use the interesting-decision test as the literal design filter; (2) reach 'enveloping complexity' via PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE (and the existing Encyclopedia/Codex as just-in-time tutorial) — but remember Civ is turn-based; its breadth must be trimmed to fit a real-time flow budget.

precedents.name: Pax Pamir / elegant euro-style designs (depth-without-complexity exemplar)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Very lean rules and simple individual actions, yet opaque, rich emergent strategy — the 'easy to learn, hard to master' ideal.
precedents.outcome: Held up in design discourse as the model of high depth from low complexity.
precedents.lessonForUs: Proves the target is achievable: maximize viable-strategy count per rule, not rule count. For each new OpenRA system, ask 'does this add emergent depth or just surface complexity?' and prefer the lean design that yields opaque, replayable strategy.

psychology.detail:
FRAMEWORK-BY-FRAMEWORK ANALYSIS

1) SID MEIER — 'a game is a series of interesting decisions.' A decision is interesting iff (a) no option is clearly dominant, (b) options are not equally attractive, (c) the player can make an informed choice. The current loop fails all three, which is the rigorous reason it feels shallow. This is the project's primary design filter: every faction, unit, building, and strategic system must pass this test or it is decoration. (gamedeveloper.com Sid Meier GDC 2012; bosnan.net Sid Meier essay; oreilly Players Making Decisions Part 3.)

2) KOSTER — THEORY OF FUN. Fun = the brain's reward for mastering new patterns; games are learning machines; they go boring the moment the pattern is mastered. The dominant-strategy problem is fatal here: a solved game has exactly one pattern to learn, so fun is exhausted in a few sessions. Differentiated factions and cross-coupled systems create MORE patterns to master, extending the fun curve — but only if those patterns are genuinely distinct, not reskins. (befreed.ai; shortform.com Theory of Fun summaries.)

3) CSIKSZENTMIHALYI — FLOW. Fun lives in the channel where challenge ≈ skill; above it = anxiety, below = boredom. The real-time constraint is the whole ballgame: 4X depth raises challenge-per-second, and unlike turn-based games there's no pause to absorb it. The design must therefore RAISE skill gradually (progressive disclosure/scaffolding) and CAP challenge-per-second (decision budget, automation) to keep players in-channel. (yukaichou.com flow guide; Jenova Chen 'Flow in Games' thesis; thinkgamedesign.com.)

4) MDA (Hunicke/LeBlanc/Zubek) + SCHELL. Designers build bottom-up (mechanics) but players experience top-down (aesthetics). The user's goals are aesthetic ('engaging,' 'enveloping,' 'meaningful'). The method: target the aesthetic, find the minimal mechanics whose dynamics produce it, validate by playtest, cut mechanics that don't pay off. Schell's Lens of Meaningful Choices = the operational checklist (count real choices; verify none dominant; verify the player understands stakes). (en.wikipedia.org MDA; firstpersonscholar.com working theory; game-developers.org MDA.)

5) DEPTH vs COMPLEXITY / ELEGANCE. Complexity = rules to track (cost). Depth = viable strategies that emerge (payoff). Elegant design maximizes depth/complexity (Pax Pamir, Go). The vision's central risk is conflating the two — adding complexity and assuming depth. The antidote is system INTERACTION over system MULTIPLICATION: a few cross-coupled systems yield combinatorial depth; many parallel meters yield tedium. (BGG complexity-vs-AP thread; acrosstheboardcafe.com; leagueofgamemakers.com AP series.)

6) ANALYSIS PARALYSIS / COGNITIVE LOAD. Too many options inhibit deliberate (System 2) thinking; in real time this is catastrophic — it doesn't slow the player, it breaks them. Documented remedies: limit simultaneous choices, automate the obvious, disclose progressively, ensure consequences are legible. (medium theuglymonster AP; nerdlab-games 15 ways to reduce AP; learningloop AP.)

7) THE 4X ENDGAME / STELLARIS TRAP. Structural, not incidental: interfaces tuned for the early game collapse under late-game numbers where each decision matters less but costs the same time; automation underperforms manual play, forcing 'tedium vs inefficiency.' A real-time game amplifies this. Implication: cap/abstract scaling, automate size-scaling tasks penalty-free, and keep match arcs short enough to resolve before the tedium threshold. (civfanatics 'boring endgame' essay; Stellaris Steam/Paradox micromanagement threads.)

8) DEATHBALL/DOOMSTACK. The big-army expression of the dominant-strategy disease. Counters are well documented and directly buildable in OpenRA: give top-tier units exploitable vulnerabilities so they need cheaper screens (forces composition), make territory/objectives reward splitting forces (Company of Heroes), and make pure top-tier stacks cost-inefficient. Shifts the skill axis to positioning/combined-arms — modern feel without an APM grind. (Paradox deathball thread; redbull Dota 2 deathball; MWO deathball thread.)

9) ENGINE REALITY (verified in-repo). Present and cheap to prototype against: SupportPowers/ traits, Encyclopedia.cs + EncyclopediaLogic.cs (host for the real-ore Codex AND a just-in-time tutorial), diplomacy/stances, prerequisites/tech-tree, veterancy, Lua scripting (mission/strategic-layer logic). The expensive constraint is 32-facing sprite art per new unit — so sequence cheap-to-change systems (YAML/Lua, placeholder art) ahead of expensive-to-change art, and gate art spend on proven fun.

BOTTOM LINE (skeptical): The vision can absolutely be fun, and the user's diagnosis is correct. But 'add diplomacy + research + economy + real factions' is not a fun guarantee — it is a coin flip whose outcome is decided by ONE thing: whether each addition produces interesting, differentiated, non-dominated decisions that interact with the core loop (depth) or merely more rules and clicks (complexity). Treat fun as an engineering constraint with explicit tests (decision budget, no-dominant-strategy lens, automate-the-tedium, progressive disclosure), prototype the strategic layer fast in YAML/Lua before funding art, and let playtest metrics — not enthusiasm — decide what ships.

SOURCES: gamedeveloper.com (Sid Meier GDC 2012 'interesting decisions'); bosnan.net/essays/sid-meier; oreilly.com Players Making Decisions Part 3; befreed.ai & shortform.com (Koster Theory of Fun); yukaichou.com flow guide, jenovachen.com Flow in Games thesis, thinkgamedesign.com (Csikszentmihalyi flow); en.wikipedia.org MDA framework, firstpersonscholar.com working theory of game design, game-developers.org MDA (Hunicke/Schell); medium.com/theuglymonster, nerdlab-games.com, leagueofgamemakers.com, boardgamegeek.com (analysis paralysis / depth vs complexity / Pax Pamir elegance); simonhalliday.com & liquipedia (StarCraft 2 asymmetric design, macro/micro); forum.paradoxplaza.com & redbull.com & mwomercs.com (deathball/doomstack); forums.civfanatics.com & steamcommunity.com Stellaris discussions (4X late-game tedium); gamerant.com & greedygoblinblog & frontrowcrew (Company of Heroes/Northgard territory control, RTS without micro); ixdf.org, uxpin.com, nngroup-style progressive disclosure sources (onboarding/cognitive load).

hybrids.executiveSummary: The user's vision — "an RTS with 4X depth that is real-time, fast, and engaging, with real countries differentiated by strategic use, meaningful diplomacy/research/defense, and a strategic-resources codex" — is almost exactly the design brief that Rise of Nations (2003) shipped against, and largely solved. RoN is the closest north star by a wide margin: it is literally "Civ meets StarCraft," it ran real-time, and Brian Reynolds (Civ II / Alpha Centauri designer) explicitly compressed 4X depth into RTS pacing using three load-bearing inventions — (1) national borders/territory that gate where you build, (2) attrition that punishes undefended invasion (turning "defense" into a real strategic system instead of static turtling), and (3) self-sufficient cities + macro-only economy that kill worker micro. Sins of a Solar Empire is the second north star and proves the genre is commercially durable, but it bought its 4X depth by slowing down to a multi-hour pace — the exact thing the user wants to avoid. The genre's graveyard is real: RTS+4X hybrids are notorious for being "neither fish nor fowl," failing the pacing test because real-time strips away the player's control over when to think. The single most important lesson across every precedent is this: DO NOT add 4X depth by adding things the player must constantly manage. Add depth by making a SMALL number of decisions matter MORE (Company of Heroes' decision-density model), automating everything that is busywork (Supreme Commander / RoN economy), and letting systems run themselves once configured. The user's instinct to "tone down" Civ/Stellaris is correct and is the whole ballgame; the danger is not too little depth, it is too much management. OpenRA is unusually well-positioned to attempt this because it already ships the hard parts (prerequisite tech tree, support powers, diplomacy stances, encyclopedia widget, data-driven traits), so the work is design and YAML/trait composition, not new engine systems.
keyFindings: RISE OF NATIONS IS THE NORTH STAR. It is the only widely-loved game that hit the exact target — real-time, fast (20–60 min matches), with Civ-style ages, a research library, territory/borders, attrition, diplomacy (Peace/War/Allied), wonders, rare strategic resources you scout and fight over, and 18 nations each with 4–8 unique units. Its designer was the Civ II / Alpha Centauri lead. Studying RoN is not optional; it is the reference implementation of this exact vision.

THE GENRE'S CORE FAILURE MODE IS PACING, NOT DEPTH. Multiple sources converge: in real-time you do NOT control when the game lets you think, so bolting a big 4X tech tree + diplomacy + empire management onto an RTS produces 'neither fish nor fowl' — it fails at RTS reflexes AND at 4X contemplation. Every hour spent must be earned against this trap.

DEPTH MUST COME FROM DECISION DENSITY, NOT MANAGEMENT LOAD. Company of Heroes is the antithesis of unit-spam and the model to copy: small squad counts, contextual resources captured by holding connected territory sectors (no harvesting/worker micro), so each unit and each map-control decision is heavy. This is exactly how to replace the user's hated loop ('make troops, attack/defend, repeat') without slowing the game down.

AUTOMATE THE ECONOMY OR DIE. RoN cities become self-reliant (no worker reassignment like StarCraft); Supreme Commander uses streaming income/expenditure with build queues so you manage a flow, not clicks; CoH puts resources on territory not harvesters. Every successful fast-but-deep game removed economic busywork so the player's attention is free for strategy. OpenRA's classic ore-harvester loop is the busywork to minimize.

ATTRITION + BORDERS IS THE SINGLE BEST IDEA TO STEAL FOR 'MORE INTERESTING DEFENSE.' RoN's attrition (enemy units take continuous damage inside your borders unless supplied) and territory (you can only build in your borders) together convert defense from passive turtling into an active strategic system — supply lines, border expansion, forts — directly serving the user's goal of meaningful defense and replacing the shallow attack/defend loop.

RESEARCH MUST BE FEW BIG CHOICES, FAST, NOT MANY SMALL ONES, SLOW. Stellaris' and Civ's well-documented mid/late-game tedium comes from endless small incremental techs, resource-accumulation waiting, and snowballing that auto-decides the game. For a fast game: shallow, branching, mutually-exclusive research with visible identity-shaping payoffs (pick a doctrine, not 200 +5% upgrades). Empire Earth's 3-branch university (military/economy/empire) and RoN's compact library are better templates than Civ's full tree.

REAL-NATION FACTIONS = ASYMMETRY BY STRATEGIC USE, AND RoN ALREADY PROVES THE PATTERN. RoN's 18 nations differ by unique units + unique bonuses + a power that nudges strategy (e.g., a nation that gathers a resource from turn one). The user's 'each country needs ≥1 unique troop and ≥1 unique building' is a sound, RoN-validated minimum; the bigger win is a single signature MECHANIC per nation that biases its strategy (rush / economy / defense / tech), which is cheaper than many unique units (which cost the most — 32-facing sprite art).

THE TWO-LAYER (TOTAL WAR) MODEL IS A TRAP FOR THIS PROJECT. Total War's turn-based campaign + real-time battle works but requires building TWO games and a meta-layer; it also reintroduces turn-based pacing. Given OpenRA is a single-layer real-time engine and the user explicitly wants ONE fast real-time experience, the depth must live INSIDE the RTS match (RoN/Sins/CoH model), not in a separate strategic layer.

SINS PROVES DURABILITY BUT AT THE WRONG SPEED. Sins ('RT4X') successfully fused research/diplomacy/empire-management in real time and spawned a 2024 sequel, but it is deliberately slow (hours-long), uses seamless strategic zoom, an Empire Tree UI to tame scale, and pacts/diplomacy-victory. Borrow its UI-scaling and diplomacy-incentive ideas; reject its tempo.

TENSION IS A SUBSTITUTE FOR SLOWNESS. Northgard and They Are Billions create 'depth feel' through escalating pressure (escalating expansion costs, food upkeep, random events, the swarm) rather than menu depth. A fast game can feel strategically rich via well-placed tension/risk decisions (when to expand, when to commit) instead of more spreadsheets — cheap to build in OpenRA via map scripting/Lua and trait conditions.
recommendations: Adopt Rise of Nations as the explicit north star and Company of Heroes as the secondary lens. Write the design doc as 'RoN's strategic systems (borders, attrition, ages, rare resources, library, diplomacy) expressed through CoH's low-unit-count, high-decision-density combat and territory economy.' Sins for UI-at-scale and diplomacy incentives; reject its tempo.

Make depth come from FEWER, HEAVIER decisions — never from more things to micromanage. Concretely: cap practical army sizes, raise per-unit value, and route resources through territory control rather than harvesters. Replace the ore-harvester grind: tie income to holding connected map sectors (CoH/RoN), so the strategic map IS the economy.

Steal the borders+attrition pair to deliver the user's 'more interesting defense.' Implement a territory/ownership layer; allow building only in owned territory; apply continuous attrition damage to enemies inside your borders unless they bring supply. OpenRA can model this with area-ownership traits + a periodic damage warhead/condition + a supply unit that suppresses it. This single system converts defense from turtling into strategy.

Design research as a SHALLOW branching doctrine tree with mutually-exclusive choices and fast completion, not a deep incremental tech list. Aim for a handful of identity-defining picks per match (e.g., 3 branches like Empire Earth: Military / Economy / Statecraft) that visibly change how the nation plays. Avoid hundreds of +X% upgrades and avoid resource-accumulation waiting (the Stellaris/Civ tedium trap). OpenRA's existing prerequisite system can express this directly in YAML.

Differentiate nations primarily by ONE signature strategic mechanic each, plus the required unique troop + unique building — not by piles of unique units. Sprite art (32 facings) is the cost ceiling, so spend it where it changes strategy most. Map each real country to a doctrine bias (e.g., a fast-mobilization rusher, an economic/industrial power, a defensive/fortification power, a tech/precision power) so they are 'balanced but differentiated by strategic use,' exactly as the user wants.

Keep it ONE real-time layer. Do not build a Total-War-style separate turn-based campaign/meta map — it doubles scope, fights the engine, and reintroduces the turn-based pacing the user is trying to escape. All 4X depth lives inside the live match.

Use ages/epochs as the pacing spine and the 'progression' hook, but keep them few and meaningful (think AoE's 4 ages, not Empire Earth's 15). Each age advance should unlock a visible new strategic option and re-open the rock-paper-scissors, giving the satisfying 'power up' beat without slowing the match. This also frames the 'contemporary/modern military tech' fantasy cleanly.

Inject tension instead of length to feel deep without being slow. Use escalating expansion costs (Northgard), supply/upkeep pressure, and scripted strategic events via Lua so players make high-stakes timing decisions (commit/expand/turtle) in real time. This is the cheapest credible source of 'Civ-like envelopment' on the OpenRA engine.

Lean hard on the existing Encyclopedia widget for the strategic-resources Codex AND as a teaching tool for the new systems. Document each real ore/strategic resource and what it enables; the Codex doubles as onboarding for borders/attrition/doctrines, which is essential because added depth raises the learning cliff — the #1 churn risk for hybrids.

De-risk with a vertical slice before broad content: prototype ONE new system (territory+attrition economy) with the existing RA art and 2 nations, in pure YAML/traits, and playtest match length and decision density. Prove the core loop is fast AND deep before commissioning expensive new 32-facing sprites for many countries.
risks: 'Neither fish nor fowl' pacing failure: the documented #1 killer of RTS+4X hybrids. If 4X depth is added as management load, the game becomes too busy to be a good RTS and too rushed to be a good 4X, satisfying no one. Mitigate by holding the line on decision-density-not-management-load.

Micromanagement creep: every new system (borders, supply, research, diplomacy) tempts per-unit/per-tick fiddling. Without aggressive automation (self-running cities, build queues, area-based economy) the player drowns and the game slows — the opposite of the goal.

Snowball/runaway leader: Stellaris and RoN both show that economic or tech leads can auto-decide matches. Fast games are especially punishing here because there's no slow turn-based recovery. Needs comeback mechanics (CoH's manpower-on-HQ, attrition-aided defense, catch-up bands) baked in from the start.

Art-cost ceiling on factions: unique units need 32-facing sprites — the real bottleneck. Promising many real countries each with multiple unique units risks an unfinishable content backlog. Differentiate by mechanics/bonuses first; ration unique sprites.

Learning-cliff / onboarding churn: more strategic systems = steeper ramp. OpenRA's audience expects pick-up-and-play RTS. Without strong tutorialization (Codex, telegraphed systems), added depth becomes friction that loses players.

Determinism constraints: borders, attrition-over-time, supply, and economy-from-territory all run inside world.Tick() and must use fixed-point math and synced state (no float/Random/wall-clock) or they desync in lock-step multiplayer. Several proposed systems are tick-driven and must be implemented per OpenRA's determinism rules.

Balancing real nations is politically and mechanically fraught: tying factions to real militaries invites both balance complaints and sensitivity issues; 'realistic' asymmetry can produce dominant strategies. Plan for abstraction and iterative balance passes.

Scope/identity drift: trying to honor Civ (research), Stellaris (diplomacy/depth), CoH (territory), and RoN (everything) at once can blur the design. The mitigation is to commit to RoN as the single north star and treat the others as targeted organ donors, not co-equal templates.

precedents.name: Rise of Nations (2003) — THE NORTH STAR
precedents.whatTheyDid: Brian Reynolds (Civ II / Alpha Centauri) built a literal real-time Civilization: ages/epochs, a Library research tree, national borders that gate construction, attrition that damages unsupplied enemies inside your territory, diplomacy (Peace/War/Allied), wonders, rare strategic resources you scout/expand toward and fight over, and 18 nations each with 4–8 unique units plus unique bonuses. Crucially it removed worker micro (cities become self-sufficient) and discouraged focus-fire so attention goes to macro/strategy.
precedents.outcome: Critical and commercial success; widely regarded as the best 'Civ-in-real-time' ever made and the genre's high-water mark for compressing 4X depth into fast (20–60 min) matches.
precedents.lessonForUs: This is the exact vision already shipped and validated. Copy its three load-bearing systems wholesale — borders, attrition, self-running economy — and its differentiation pattern (unique unit + unique bonus + a strategy-biasing power per nation). It maps 1:1 onto the user's 'real countries, unique troop+building, strategic resources + codex, meaningful defense, real-time-but-deep.'

precedents.name: Sins of a Solar Empire (2008) / Sins II (2024) — the 'RT4X' proof
precedents.whatTheyDid: Self-described 'RT4X': fully real-time, but with two-tree research (military/civic), real diplomacy (pacts giving economy/research/military bonuses; diplomatic victory), planet management, and grand scale tamed by seamless strategic zoom and an Empire Tree UI.
precedents.outcome: Cult-classic success, durable enough to get a 2024 sequel praised as a great 4X-RTS. But matches run for HOURS — it bought depth with slowness.
precedents.lessonForUs: Proves the fusion is durable and that UI (zoom + an empire-overview tree) is what makes real-time scale playable. Borrow its diplomacy-as-positive-incentive design and its scaling UI; REJECT its tempo. It is the cautionary counter-example to the user's 'fast and engaging' requirement.

precedents.name: Company of Heroes (2006) — the anti-spam model
precedents.whatTheyDid: Replaced base-building/harvester economy with contextual resources captured by holding connected territory sectors (cut off a point and you starve the enemy's supply line). Emphasized small squads, cover, and flanking over mass armies; put core resource on the HQ to enable comebacks.
precedents.outcome: Landmark critical success; the benchmark for high-decision-density, low-unit-count RTS.
precedents.lessonForUs: This is the cure for the user's hated loop and the way to add depth WITHOUT slowing down: fewer units that matter more, and an economy that IS map control. Make the strategic map the resource system; raise per-unit value; build in comeback potential.

precedents.name: Empire Earth (2001) & Age of Empires — ages/epochs done two ways
precedents.whatTheyDid: AoE: a tight handful of ages, each a clear power spike re-opening the rock-paper-scissors. Empire Earth: up to 15 epochs and a 3-branch university (military/economy/empire) with 'crown' rewards for racing a branch.
precedents.outcome: AoE's restraint = timeless and readable; Empire Earth's sprawl = impressive but bloated and less balanced.
precedents.lessonForUs: Use ages as the pacing spine and progression hook, but keep them FEW (AoE-style ~4, not EE's 15). Empire Earth's clean 3-branch research split is a great compact template for fast, identity-shaping research; its scale is a warning.

precedents.name: Northgard (2017) & They Are Billions (2019) — tension as depth
precedents.whatTheyDid: Northgard: territory claimed tile-by-tile at EXPONENTIALLY escalating food cost, building caps per tile forcing spread, food upkeep that scales with population, plus random events (famine, invasions). They Are Billions: relentless escalating swarm pressure forcing planning and rapid response.
precedents.outcome: Both beloved for feeling tense and strategically rich without big menus or slow turns.
precedents.lessonForUs: You can manufacture 'depth feel' and Civ-like envelopment via PRESSURE and risk-timing decisions rather than management surface area. Escalating expansion costs and upkeep are cheap, potent ways to make real-time expansion a real decision. Easy to script in OpenRA via Lua + trait conditions.

precedents.name: Total War series — the two-layer model (a road NOT to take)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Split the game cleanly: turn-based campaign map (economy, diplomacy, politics) feeds into real-time tactical battles; the layers interconnect (bad economy → unrest → weaker battles).
precedents.outcome: Hugely successful, but it is effectively two games plus a meta-layer, and the strategy layer is turn-based.
precedents.lessonForUs: Tempting but wrong for THIS project: it doubles scope, fights OpenRA's single real-time engine, and reintroduces turn-based pacing. Keep all 4X depth inside the live real-time match. Note only the principle: strategic context must give battles 'consequence.'

precedents.name: Supreme Commander (2007) — economy automation at scale
precedents.whatTheyDid: Streaming income/expenditure of mass+energy (manage a flow, not clicks), big build queues, and strategic zoom from one soldier to the whole theater — designed so huge scale doesn't mean huge micro.
precedents.outcome: Acclaimed for macro elegance; proof you can run an enormous game without per-unit babysitting.
precedents.lessonForUs: To add economic depth without slowing the game, model income/expense as a managed FLOW with queues and automation, and invest in zoom/overview UI so scale stays legible. Directly informs how to make a deeper economy that is still fast.

precedents.name: Stellaris & Civilization — what to SPEED UP / avoid
precedents.whatTheyDid: Deep incremental tech trees, influence/resource-accumulation gates on diplomacy and expansion, tall vs wide systems, wonders.
precedents.outcome: Beloved for depth but plagued by well-documented mid/late-game tedium: waiting on resource accumulation, hundreds of marginal techs, and snowballing that auto-decides the game.
precedents.lessonForUs: This is the explicit DON'T. Compress research to few big branching choices that resolve fast; never gate action behind slow resource accumulation; design anti-snowball/comeback mechanics up front. The user's instinct to 'tone it down' is precisely correct — these games show what happens when you don't.

# RTS-with-4X-Depth: Precedent Analysis for a Contemporary OpenRA

## The verdict up front
The user has, perhaps without knowing it, described **Rise of Nations** almost feature-for-feature. RoN is the closest north star and should be the explicit reference design. **Company of Heroes** is the secondary lens (how to get depth without spam or slowdown). **Sins of a Solar Empire** proves the hybrid is durable but is the cautionary example on tempo. Everything else is an organ donor for one specific idea.

## The genre's central problem (read this first)
RTS+4X hybrids are infamous as 'neither fish nor fowl.' The root cause is **pacing control**: in a 4X/grand-strategy game the player decides when to stop and think; in real-time the game decides for them. Bolting a large tech tree + diplomacy + empire management onto a real-time game tends to make it simultaneously too frantic to contemplate and too contemplative to be a crisp RTS. Sources repeatedly note that 'actual strategy is made impossible when you don't have time to make strategic decisions.' Therefore the prime directive for this project is:

> **Add depth by making a SMALL number of decisions matter MORE — never by adding more things to manage per second.**

This is the through-line that connects every successful precedent below and is the answer to the user's stated goal of replacing 'make troops, attack/defend, repeat.'

## How each precedent handled diplomacy / research / economy / territory in (near) real time

**Rise of Nations — the reference implementation.**
- *Territory:* 'National borders.' You can only build inside your territory (or an ally's). Borders expand via cities, forts, tech, and capturing rare resources. This makes map space a first-class strategic resource and makes expansion a deliberate act.
- *Defense via attrition:* once researched, enemy units take continuous damage inside your borders unless they bring supply wagons. This is the single most elegant 'interesting defense' mechanic in the genre — it converts turtling into an active supply-line/border game and gives boomers a real defense without static cheese.
- *Economy without micro:* cities, once set up, are self-reliant — no StarCraft-style worker reassignment. Focus-firing the same target is penalized, pushing attention to macro decisions. This is how RoN stayed fast despite Civ-like breadth.
- *Research:* a compact Library tree across ages, not Civ's sprawling tree — fewer, meatier choices.
- *Diplomacy:* Peace / War / Allied, simple and readable.
- *Resources + the user's Codex:* basic resources plus **rare/strategic resources** scattered on the map that you scout for, must hold inside your borders, and that grant economic/military bonuses. This is exactly the 'real-life ores / strategic resources surfaced via a codex' vision — RoN already did the gameplay half.
- *Factions:* 18 nations, each 4–8 unique units plus unique bonuses/powers that bias strategy. This validates the user's 'each country needs a unique troop and building' as a sound minimum, and points to the cheaper, higher-leverage move: one signature mechanic per nation.

**Company of Heroes — depth via decision density, the antithesis of spam.**
- *Territory = economy:* resources (manpower/fuel/munitions) come from capturing connected territory sectors; cut a link and you sever the enemy's supply. No harvesters, no worker micro. Holding the map IS the economy.
- *Low unit count, high unit value:* small squads, cover, flanking. Every unit and every capture is a heavy decision. Core resource on the HQ enables comebacks.
- *Lesson:* this is the precise template for replacing OpenRA's shallow spam loop while keeping the game fast.

**Sins of a Solar Empire — 'RT4X', durable but slow.**
- Real-time research (military/civic trees), genuine diplomacy (pacts granting economy/research/military bonuses; diplomatic victory), planet management — all live. Tamed grand scale with **seamless strategic zoom** and an **Empire Tree** overview UI. Got a well-reviewed 2024 sequel.
- *But* matches run for hours. Borrow its UI-scaling and positive-incentive diplomacy; reject its tempo.

**Empire Earth & Age of Empires — ages/epochs.**
- AoE: a few ages, each a clear power spike that re-opens combat counters — restrained and timeless. Empire Earth: up to 15 epochs and a clean 3-branch university (military/economy/empire) with 'crown' rewards for racing a branch — impressive but bloated.
- *Lesson:* use ages as the pacing spine and the progression dopamine, but keep them FEW (AoE-style). EE's 3-branch research split is a great compact model; its 15-epoch sprawl is the warning.

**Northgard & They Are Billions — tension instead of length.**
- Northgard: tile-by-tile territory at exponentially escalating food cost, per-tile build caps forcing spread, scaling upkeep, random events. They Are Billions: escalating swarm pressure. Both feel deep and tense without menus or slow turns.
- *Lesson:* manufacture strategic richness through pressure and risk-timing (when to expand/commit/turtle), which is cheap to script in OpenRA via Lua and trait conditions.

**Total War — the two-layer model to AVOID here.**
- Turn-based campaign (economy/diplomacy/politics) feeding real-time battles, with interconnection (bad economy → unrest → weaker battles). Great, but it is two games + a meta-layer and the strategy layer is turn-based. For a single-layer real-time engine and a 'fast' goal, keep all depth inside the live match.

**Supreme Commander — economy as a managed flow.**
- Streaming mass/energy income vs expenditure, big queues, strategic zoom. Huge scale without per-unit babysitting.
- *Lesson:* deeper economy without slowdown = model income/expense as a flow with queues + automation, and invest in overview/zoom UI.

**Stellaris & Civilization — the explicit DON'Ts.**
- Deep incremental tech, diplomacy/expansion gated behind slow resource (influence) accumulation, snowballing that auto-decides games, documented mid/late-game tedium ('waiting around,' 'numbers ballooning'). The user's instinct to 'tone it down' is exactly right; these show the failure if you don't.

## Translating this onto OpenRA specifically
OpenRA already ships the expensive prerequisites: a prerequisite/tech-tree system (perfect for a shallow branching doctrine tree in YAML), support powers (for nation signature abilities), veterancy, diplomacy stances (Peace/War/Allied is already conceptually there), an in-game editor, Lua scripting (for tension events and territory logic), and an Encyclopedia widget (the Codex). So the dominant work is **design + YAML/trait composition**, not new engine subsystems — with three caveats:
1. **Territory + attrition + territory-based economy are tick-driven and run inside world.Tick()** → must use fixed-point WPos/WDist math and [Sync] state, no float/Random/wall-clock, per OpenRA's determinism rules, or lock-step multiplayer desyncs.
2. **Art is the ceiling.** Unique units need 32-facing sprites. Differentiate nations by mechanics/bonuses first; ration unique sprites.
3. **Onboarding is mandatory.** More systems = steeper ramp; lean on the Codex to teach borders/attrition/doctrines.

## Recommended one-line framing for the design doc
**"Rise of Nations' strategic systems (borders, attrition, ages, rare strategic resources, a compact research library, simple diplomacy) expressed through Company of Heroes' low-unit-count, territory-is-economy, high-decision-density combat — kept to a single real-time layer, with Sins' overview UI and Supreme Commander's flow-economy automation to keep it fast."**

Sources: Rise of Nations design/territory/attrition/rare-resources (gamedeveloper.com retrospective; riseofnations.fandom.com; en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rise_of_Nations; ron.heavengames.com); Sins RT4X (en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sins_of_a_Solar_Empire; pcgamer.com); Company of Heroes territory/squad design (companyofheroes.fandom.com; gamespot.com designer diary; pcgamer.com making-of); Empire Earth/AoE epochs (empireearth.fandom.com; ageofempires.fandom.com); Northgard/TAB tension (denistodorovhonours.wordpress.com; northgard.fandom.com; gamepressure.com); Total War two-layer (totalwar.fandom.com; gamedeveloper.com; gdcvault.com); Supreme Commander economy (supcom.fandom.com); Stellaris/Civ pacing critiques (steamcommunity.com Stellaris discussions; forum.paradoxplaza.com; forums.civfanatics.com); hybrid 'neither fish nor fowl' pacing problem (gamedeveloper.com; resetera.com; eneba.com 4X overview).

diplomacy.executiveSummary:
OpenRA already has the hard half of diplomacy: per-player Ally/Enemy/Neutral relationships stored as mutable bitmasks (Player.cs: AlliedPlayersMask/EnemyPlayersMask), set once at game start from lobby teams (CreateMapPlayers.cs) and never changed in-game. There is no order, no UI, and no asymmetry-handling for runtime relationship changes — that absence is the entire opportunity. The job is NOT to bolt a 4X negotiation screen onto an RTS; it is to make relationships a *live, fast, consequence-bearing resource* you spend and risk in real time, the way you already spend money and APM.

The design rests on five pillars. (1) Extend the 3-state stance into a small, fixed set of *binding, timed agreements* — Ceasefire, Non-Aggression Pact (NAP), Alliance, Defensive Pact, Trade Route, Vision Share, Vassalage — each a synced Order, each with a visible timer or break-cost, none requiring a text negotiation. (2) Make agreements MATTER mechanically by attaching concrete bonuses to them (shared vision uncovers map, trade routes give passive income, alliances enable shared control), so a pact is a build-order decision, not flavor. (3) Solve the "diplomacy is pointless in 1v1" problem by introducing NEUTRAL MINOR FACTIONS / city-states on the map that BOTH players can bribe, ally, or conquer — this injects a third party into every match including 1v1 and skirmish-vs-AI, converting diplomacy from "talk to your one opponent" (degenerate) into "race your opponent for the loyalty of three minors" (always live). (4) Make betrayal a first-class, *rewarding-but-priced* action: breaking a pact early is always allowed (you are never locked in), but it triggers a telegraphed "Treaty Broken" warning to the victim with a few seconds of grace, plus a lasting Trust penalty that minors and AI remember and price into future deals. (5) Drive the whole thing through a lightweight radial / one-click quick-offer UI on the existing diplomacy panel and player portraits — offers are pre-baked templates (like production items), accepted/declined with one click and a countdown, never free-text. Against AI, opponents evaluate offers with a transparent opinion score (Sins/Stellaris model) so the player can *read* the AI and the AI can plausibly accept. The headline anti-stalemate rule: alliances and NAPs are *time-boxed and decay* — permanent peace is impossible, so the map always trends back toward conflict, which is what keeps an RTS fast.
keyFindings: ENGINE FIT IS EXCELLENT. OpenRA's relationship model (OpenRA.Game/Player.cs lines 91-93: PlayerMask, AlliedPlayersMask, EnemyPlayersMask as LongBitSet) is already per-player and ASYMMETRIC-capable — p can ally q without q allying p. RelationshipWith() (line 249) just tests mask overlap. So 'I offered, you haven't accepted' and 'I betrayed you but you still think we're allied' are both representable for free. The masks are public and directly assignable; the only missing pieces are a synced Order to mutate them and a UI to issue it.

RELATIONSHIPS ARE SET ONCE AND FROZEN. CreateMapPlayers.cs (lines 142-174, SetupPlayerMasks) populates the masks at world-load from lobby teams/map Allies-Enemies lists, then nothing in the engine ever changes them. There is no in-game ally/unally command in the base engine (the existing 'StanceSelectorLogic' is UNIT stance — hold-fire/return-fire — not diplomatic stance). This is a greenfield surface, not a refactor.

THE 1v1 / SKIRMISH PROBLEM IS REAL AND WELL-DOCUMENTED. In a pure 1v1 the only diplomatic move is peace-with-your-sole-opponent, which is either irrelevant or a draw — diplomacy has nothing to act on. Research on kingmaking (Skeleton Code Machine, BGDF) confirms FFA diplomacy is 'cursed' because group politics overrides individual skill. The fix used by every game where diplomacy matters in small matches is the SAME: put third parties on the board (Rise of Nations minor nations, Sins minor factions/militia, Stellaris pre-FTL/marauders). A neutral you can court gives diplomacy an object even in 1v1.

BINDING + TIMED IS WHAT MAKES IT FAST. Rise of Nations gates alliances behind being at-peace and uses tribute as the currency; Sins makes pacts 'always-on passive bonuses that don't go away unless one side ends it'; Stellaris time-boxes truces and adds war exhaustion so wars self-terminate. The common thread: agreements are STATE you toggle, with mechanical payloads and natural expiry — not conversations. That maps perfectly onto OpenRA's Order + support-power-timer + INotify pattern.

OPINION/RELATIONS SCORE IS HOW AI DIPLOMACY BECOMES READABLE. Sins shows relation factors on hover (same race +, adjacency -, donations +, military action -); Stellaris envoys move opinion -400..+400. A single transparent integer 'opinion' per AI/minor, with itemized contributors shown on hover, lets the human PREDICT acceptance and lets a simple deterministic AI accept/decline without 'feeling random' — critical in a lockstep engine where true randomness is banned anyway.

SHARED CONTROL IS A KNOWN, BELOVED ALLIANCE PAYLOAD. Warcraft 3's 'Advanced Shared Unit Control' (control allies' units without changing owner) is the single most-cited alliance feature and the backbone of its famous 'Diplomacy' custom mode ('the point is to constantly BETRAY your friends'). OpenRA can model this as an alliance-tier permission flag without transferring Actor ownership — high value, moderate cost.

BETRAYAL IS THE FUN ENGINE, BUT NEEDS FRICTION, NOT A LOCK. The WC3 Diplomacy mode is explicitly built around betrayal and is wildly popular precisely because trust is fragile and earned. The design lesson: never PREVENT betrayal (that kills the tension), but TELEGRAPH it (victim gets a warning + grace window so it's a skill/timing play, not a free backstab) and PRICE it (a persistent Trust stat that minors and AI remember). Surprise-with-counterplay beats both 'no betrayal' and 'free betrayal'.

TEAM/FFA TEAMPLAY ALREADY HAS MECHANICAL HOOKS. CoH/Wargame show shared vision, shared/parallel income, and combined-arms spotting are what make team RTS deep. OpenRA already has shroud per-player (RevealsShroud/Shroud traits) and resource storage per-player, so 'Vision Share' and 'Trade Route income' pacts are small, well-scoped trait additions rather than new subsystems.
recommendations: SHIP A FIXED MENU OF 7 AGREEMENT TYPES, NOT FREE NEGOTIATION. Ceasefire (short timed truce, units won't auto-target — reuse AutoTarget relationship checks), NAP (longer 'we won't attack, no shared bonuses' — the cheap default), Alliance (shared vision + shared control + shared production-queue visibility), Defensive Pact (auto-flips you to war if your partner is attacked — the anti-gang tool), Trade Route (both sides get +X passive credits/min while a physical trade convoy or link survives — gives a raidable target), Vision Share (one-way or mutual shroud reveal), Vassalage/Protectorate (weaker player gives a cut of income + obeys for protection — the comeback/anti-elimination mechanic). Each is one synced Order with an enum payload. This is the core deliverable.

ADD NEUTRAL MINOR FACTIONS TO MAPS AS THE UNIVERSAL DIPLOMACY OBJECT — THIS IS THE KEYSTONE. Place 1-3 non-combatant 'city-state' actors (a town, a militia outpost, an oil baron, a tech lab) owned by a Neutral player on competitive and skirmish maps. Each offers a bribe-to-ally interaction (spend credits / capture a flag / win a proximity contest) granting a concrete reward: the militia gives you a free unique unit batch, the oil baron gives +income, the tech lab unlocks a tier of tech. Both players (and AI) compete for them in real time. THIS makes diplomacy live in 1v1 and skirmish-vs-AI, where it is otherwise dead. Implement minors as ProximityCapturable + a small 'MinorFaction' trait holding an opinion/loyalty value per player; bribing raises your loyalty, the highest-loyalty player 'allies' the minor, and an enemy can out-bid or storm it militarily.

MAKE EVERY AGREEMENT TIME-BOXED OR DECAYING TO KILL STALEMATES. No permanent peace. NAPs and Alliances have a duration (e.g. 3-5 min) shown as a ring/countdown on the partner's portrait; at expiry they auto-downgrade to Neutral unless re-offered. Borrow Stellaris war-exhaustion: a long mutual peace slowly accrues 'restlessness' that minors exploit. This guarantees the map trends back to conflict and the match stays an RTS, not a frozen détente. It also means an alliance is a *deliberate, renewed* choice each time — more interesting than set-and-forget.

BUILD A ONE-CLICK QUICK-OFFER UI ON PLAYER PORTRAITS + A RADIAL — NEVER A SPREADSHEET. Click an enemy/neutral portrait -> radial of the legal agreement icons for that relationship (Ceasefire/NAP/Ally/Trade/Vision), each a single icon like a production item. Click = send offer. The recipient sees a compact toast: '[Player] offers Alliance — [Accept] [Decline]' with a countdown, dismissable with one key. Tribute/trade uses a tiny two-slider 'I give X, you give Y' popup (Rise of Nations style) capped to credits + a couple of tradeable techs — no 14-row table. Reuse the existing ProductionPaletteWidget icon-grid pattern and the support-power timer ring for cooldowns/durations.

GIVE AI A TRANSPARENT, DETERMINISTIC OPINION SCORE AND SHOW IT ON HOVER. One integer per (AI, otherPlayer) updated by deterministic events only (gifts +, attacks --, border pressure -, shared enemy +, broken treaties --). Hover the AI portrait -> itemized list of contributors (Sins/Stellaris pattern). AI accepts an offer iff opinion + offer value > a threshold that scales with how much the AI is winning (a leader is harder to ally — built-in anti-snowball). Because lockstep forbids float/Random, opinion must be integer fixed-point and event-driven — which it naturally is. This makes AI diplomacy feel intelligent and readable rather than arbitrary.

PRICE BETRAYAL WITH A TELEGRAPH + PERSISTENT TRUST STAT, NEVER A LOCK. Allow breaking any pact at any time via the same radial (set relationship to Enemy). But: (a) the victim gets a 'Treaty Broken by [Player]!' alert with a ~3-5s grace window before your units may fire on theirs (so the backstab is a timing play they can react to, not an instant free hit); (b) breaking incurs a lasting Trust hit that minor factions and AI factor into ALL future opinion checks for the rest of the match (a serial betrayer can't buy friends). This makes trust a real, spendable currency and betrayal a high-skill gamble — the core fun generator — without removing it.

USE DEFENSIVE PACTS + VASSALAGE AS THE EXPLICIT ANTI-KINGMAKING / ANTI-GANG TOOLS. Anti-gang: a Defensive Pact means if A piles on a weakened C, C's pact-partner B is auto-pulled to war with A — so ganging up has a deterrent. Anti-elimination/comeback: a near-dead player can become a Vassal (trade autonomy for survival + a protector), keeping them in the match as a meaningful actor instead of a kingmaker rage-quitting into one opponent. Cap total simultaneous alliances per player (e.g. 1-2) so the board can't collapse into one mega-bloc — the classic 'everyone allies, game stalls' failure.

IMPLEMENT IN PHASES, ART-FREE FIRST. Phase 1 (logic only, near-zero art): the SetРlayerRelationship Order, the 7-agreement enum, timers, the opinion score, and chat/hotkey triggers — fully playable and testable via map Lua (extend DiplomacyProperties.cs which today only exposes IsAlliedWith). Phase 2: the portrait radial + offer toasts (reuse existing widget chrome). Phase 3: minor factions on maps (ProximityCapturable + MinorFaction trait). Phase 4: shared-control and trade-convoy payloads. This sequences the cheap, high-impact logic before any new sprites — aligning with the project's stated art-cost ceiling. Gate the whole feature behind a map/lobby option ('Diplomacy: On/Off') so competitive 1v1 ladder play can disable it and skirmish/FFA can enable it.

EXTEND, DON'T REPLACE, THE THREE-STATE MODEL. Keep Ally/Enemy/Neutral as the ground truth the sim reads (AutoTarget, Locomotor, shroud all key off it — see Locomotor.cs line 507 using AlliedPlayersMask). Layer agreements as a SEPARATE per-pair record (type + expiry + flags) that, when it changes, simply recomputes the underlying masks. This keeps all existing combat/pathfinding/vision code untouched and determinism intact — the new system is a controller that writes the old fields, not a rewrite of them.
risks: DETERMINISM (the #1 OpenRA bug class). Every relationship change MUST go through a synced Order processed in world.Tick(), never a direct UI mutation, or clients desync. Opinion scores, timers, and minor-faction loyalty must be integer fixed-point, event-driven, and free of float/DateTime/Random (CLAUDE.md determinism rules). The offer/accept handshake is two orders (offer, then accept) and must tolerate the offer expiring or the offerer dying between them.

KINGMAKING / GANGING remain the deepest design risks. Even with Defensive Pacts and alliance caps, a losing player can still throw the game by gifting all resources to one side or suiciding into another. Mitigations (alliance caps, vassalage to keep them invested, time-boxed pacts) reduce but cannot fully eliminate this — it is inherent to multiplayer politics. Recommend disabling resource-gifting to non-allies and disabling diplomacy entirely on the ranked 1v1 ladder.

STALEMATE-BY-ALLIANCE if timers/caps are mistuned. If alliances are too cheap, too long, or uncapped, FFA collapses into one bloc and the match freezes — the opposite of the 'fast RTS' goal. The time-box + restlessness/war-exhaustion + max-alliances rules are load-bearing and need playtesting to tune, not just shipping.

UI NOISE / OFFER SPAM. Repeated offers (especially from AI or a griefing human) can flood the screen with toasts. Need a per-pair offer cooldown, a 'mute this player's offers' control, and auto-decline of duplicate pending offers. The radial must surface only LEGAL transitions for the current relationship to avoid a wall of greyed-out buttons.

AI COMPLEXITY & EXPLOITABILITY. A transparent opinion AI is readable but also gameable — players will learn to farm opinion with token gifts then betray. The persistent Trust penalty and scaling thresholds (leaders harder to befriend) are the counter, but a naive AI will still get exploited in edge cases. Budget iteration time for AI offer-evaluation tuning; consider a difficulty setting where higher AI is more suspicious of sudden generosity.

SCOPE / ART for minor factions and unique-faction shared units. Minor-faction REWARDS that grant 'a free unique unit' depend on art that may not exist yet (the project's stated 32-facing sprite ceiling). Keep Phase-3 minor rewards to art-free payloads first (credits, income %, tech unlocks, vision) and only add unit-granting minors once the relevant faction sprites exist.

BALANCE COUPLING. Trade-route income and tech-unlock minors directly affect economy and tech pacing, so diplomacy is now entangled with overall game balance — a strong trade pact could dominate. These numbers must be tuned alongside (not after) the economy and tech-tree work, or diplomacy becomes either mandatory or useless.

precedents.name: Rise of Nations (RTS diplomacy + tribute)
precedents.whatTheyDid: In-match diplomacy panel: must be at peace to propose an alliance; a two-sided tribute bar ('I give these resources / I want these') plus peace and alliance checkboxes; neutral minor nations on the map can be courted. Acceptance odds improve with good shared history.
precedents.outcome: Widely cited as one of the few RTS games where diplomacy is genuinely usable mid-match without slowing the pace; the tribute-bar UI is fast and readable.
precedents.lessonForUs: Adopt the two-slider tribute popup and the at-peace-gates-alliance rule. Crucially, adopt the MINOR NATIONS — they are why RoN diplomacy has something to do even in small games. Keep the offer surface to checkboxes/sliders, never free text.

precedents.name: Sins of a Solar Empire (real-time 4X pacts + missions + relations)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Always-on PACTS (passive bonuses that persist until one side cancels); a MISSIONS system where you pay a faction to attack a third party or bring resources; an itemized RELATIONS score shown on hover (same-race +, adjacency -, donations +, military -); unarmed Envoy ships that raise relations by presence.
precedents.outcome: Diplomacy is a viable parallel win path to military in a real-time game; the hover-itemized relations made AI behavior legible and the always-on pacts kept upkeep near zero.
precedents.lessonForUs: Copy 'pacts = always-on toggled bonuses' and 'relations score visible on hover'. The Missions idea = our 'bribe a minor/AI to attack your rival' action, a great FFA/skirmish tool. Envoy-by-presence is too slow for our pace — replace with instant click-offers.

precedents.name: Stellaris (envoys, federations, vassals, war exhaustion)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Envoys spend a slot to push opinion (-400..+400) over time; truces are time-boxed; war exhaustion forces wars to end; federations let allies vote; vassals trade autonomy for protection.
precedents.outcome: Deep and praised, BUT widely criticized as too slow/menu-heavy and for federation members voting against the player's interest — exactly the 'menu-fest' failure mode to avoid.
precedents.lessonForUs: Take the GOOD ideas — time-boxed truces, war-exhaustion-as-anti-stalemate, vassalage as a survival mechanic, opinion-over-threshold acceptance — and explicitly REJECT the slow parts: no envoy-slot micromanagement, no multi-step votes, no opinion that takes minutes to move. Our version must resolve in clicks and seconds.

precedents.name: Warcraft 3 'Diplomacy' custom mode + Advanced Shared Unit Control
precedents.whatTheyDid: Engine feature: ally settings (vision, shared control 'advanced') without transferring ownership. The community 'Diplomacy' mode is built entirely around forming and BETRAYING alliances to conquer the map, with huge armies and trading.
precedents.outcome: One of the most enduringly popular custom modes ever; betrayal IS the game and players love it precisely because trust is fragile and shared control makes alliances feel real.
precedents.lessonForUs: Ship 'shared control' as the marquee Alliance payload (permission flag, no ownership transfer). Lean INTO betrayal as the fun generator — telegraph + price it rather than prevent it. Proves players will engage deeply with real-time diplomacy when the stakes and payloads are concrete.

precedents.name: Diplomacy (the board game) + kingmaking research
precedents.whatTheyDid: Pure negotiation + simultaneous-reveal betrayal with no randomness; every alliance is non-binding and backstabbing is the whole point. Academic/design writing (Skeleton Code Machine, BGDF, DiVA thesis) analyzes why FFA diplomacy causes kingmaking.
precedents.outcome: Legendary for generating drama and broken friendships, but games are long and can stalemate; the research concludes pure-skill + group-politics is a 'cursed' combination.
precedents.lessonForUs: The drama of non-binding, breakable promises is the emotional core to capture — but the board game's pace and stalemate tendency are exactly what an RTS must avoid. Our answer: keep promises breakable (drama) but make them MECHANICALLY binding while active (instant enforcement via masks), time-boxed (no stalemate), and priced (Trust), and add minors so a losing player has someone other than a rival to throw the game to.

precedents.name: Company of Heroes / Wargame (team-RTS shared systems)
precedents.whatTheyDid: Shared/parallel income for teammates, shared vision and combined-arms spotting (one unit spots, another fires), supply-line capture points that can be cut.
precedents.outcome: Team RTS with deep, fast cooperation where vision-sharing and combined arms are the backbone of high-level play — no menus required.
precedents.lessonForUs: Model Alliance/Vision-Share payloads on these: shared shroud reveal and shared spotting are high-value, low-art, and already half-supported by OpenRA's per-player Shroud. Make Trade Routes use a physical, raidable convoy/link (like a supply line) so an alliance benefit is also an attackable target — creating new tactical objectives.
