critiques.lens: RTS pacing purist — does the 4X depth clutter and slow the fast, twitch, readable RA heartbeat the user explicitly wants to protect? Is "fast Stellaris" a contradiction the design has actually engineered around, or just asserted away?
topConcerns: ATTENTION IS THE REAL CLOCK, NOT THE MATCH TIMER — and this design overdraws it. The pacing model promises a 'single real-time layer' with no pause, but it stacks: interceptor magazine allocation + counter-battery + jam bursts + SHORAD repositioning (2-4 live defensive decisions PER assault), a diplomacy radial with countdown-ring toasts demanding accept/decline, minor-faction loyalty races, convoy-cutting/escorting, 3 stockpile counters with upkeep, era-up timing, doctrine forks, and 2-4 'pick N of M' upgrade forks — ALL while you are still expected to micro a twitch RA fight under fog. Stellaris gets away with this density precisely BECAUSE it pauses. Remove the pause but keep the decision volume and you don't get 'fast Stellaris,' you get a player who is menu-diving during the exact 8-second window a real RA fight is won or lost. The honest failure mode isn't slowness — it's that the battlefield (the thing the user loves) loses the attention competition to the dashboard.

THE ACTIVE-DEFENSE 'COST-EXCHANGE' LOOP IS ANTI-TWITCH IN DISGUISE. Framing defense as '2-4 live decisions: allocate interceptors, fire counter-battery, pop jam, reposition SHORAD' sounds like engagement, but in a no-pause RTS every one of those is an interrupt that pulls the camera and the cursor OFF your offensive micro. RA's defense is fast precisely because it's mostly autopilot (a Tesla coil just fires) — that frees your APM for the attack, which is where RTS skill expression and excitement live. Turning defense into a second active minigame doesn't add twitch; it splits the SAME hands across two fronts and, under saturation pressure (the design's own anti-turtle valve), guarantees you're babysitting magazines while your army idles. This is the StarCraft-defender's-disadvantage problem amplified.

PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE SOLVES ONBOARDING, NOT STEADY-STATE LOAD. The design leans hard on 'minute-one is just RA, systems reveal in layers' as the answer to clutter. But pacing purists care about the LATE game, not minute one. By minute 20 ALL layers are live simultaneously — and that's also when fights are biggest and twitchiest. Disclosure defers the cliff; it doesn't lower the ceiling. The '~5 actionable strategic choices on screen' budget is asserted but never reconciled with the fact that defense decisions, diplomacy toasts, and convoy threats are EVENT-DRIVEN interrupts that don't live in that 5-slot budget — they arrive unbidden, mid-fight, on the enemy's timing, not yours.

CROSS-COUPLING IS A DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD FOR PACING. 'Few systems that cross-couple' is great for depth-per-rule, but tight coupling means every fight has off-screen consequences (cut a convoy → enemy's drone doctrine starves → their AD net degrades → their minor-faction loyalty shifts). That's elegant on paper but it FORCES the player to hold the whole map's causal graph in working memory in real time. RA's genius is that a fight is mostly LOCAL — you can win the fight in front of you without modeling four other subsystems. Cross-coupling without a pause turns local twitch combat into a globally-entangled planning problem the player must solve at speed. The design's own open question (#4, 'is even 3 stockpiles too much cognitive load in real-time combat') admits this is unvalidated.

'AUTOMATE THE TEDIUM' IS LOphd-BEARING AND UNDERSPECIFIED — IT'S DOING THE WORK THE PROSE WON'T. The whole 'fast' claim rests on auto-hauling, auto-repeat production, and penalty-free automation keeping hands free. But the design never specifies WHAT stays manual, and the interesting decisions it wants to preserve (convoy routing under raid threat, interceptor allocation, SHORAD repositioning) are exactly the things that CAN'T be auto'd without becoming autopilot — i.e. the design wants them manual for 'decision density' AND wants them automated for 'speed,' which is a direct contradiction. You can't have convoy-cutting be a 'real attack vector' AND have convoy defense be penalty-free-automated. One of those two goals loses.
whatWouldFixIt: MAKE DEFENSE 'SET-AND-FORGET WITH ONE INTERRUPT,' NOT A LIVE MINIGAME. Keep the cost-exchange/saturation idea (it's genuinely good and on-theme) but resolve interception AUTOMATICALLY via pre-set target-priority toggles and auto-fired magazines. Give the defender exactly ONE optional active verb per assault (e.g. a manual 'volley/overcharge' burst on a cooldown) instead of 2-4. The strategic decision then lives BEFORE the fight (how you provisioned/positioned the net) not DURING it — which preserves twitch attention for the attack. Validate with the design's own 'late-game busywork APM' alarm: if defending raises APM during a fight, it failed.

DEMOTE DIPLOMACY TO ASYNCHRONOUS, NON-INTERRUPTING, AND DEFAULT-OFF FOR THE TWITCH AUDIENCE. The countdown-ring accept/decline toast is the single most pacing-hostile element — it's a forced, timed, mid-fight modal. Replace it with a non-blocking proposal that sits in a tray and auto-declines on expiry (no penalty for ignoring), so the player engages diplomacy ON THEIR tempo between fights, never on the opponent's. Keep the 'Diplomacy: Off' lobby toggle, and make the RANKED 1v1 mode the BALANCE-PRIMARY build (the open question #8 punts on this — pick the twitch mode as primary or the fast-RTS identity erodes).

SHIP THE THESIS AT MINIMUM VIABLE COUPLING FIRST: territory-economy + ONE stockpile + dynamic-relationship orders, and NOTHING else, then measure whether a real RA fight still feels fast with even that much off-screen entanglement. The design already proposes this MVP — make it a GATE, not a phase. If a 1v1 on the MVP already has players camera-jumping away from fights, every later system makes it strictly worse. Instrument it: track 'camera time on own army during contested fights' as a first-class pacing metric, not just the listed dominant-strategy/idle/APM alarms.

CAP EVENT-DRIVEN INTERRUPTS WITH A HARD BUDGET, same as the on-screen-choice budget. Convoy-raid alerts, diplomacy proposals, minor-faction flips, and AD-saturation warnings should be rate-limited and DEFERRABLE (a 'handle after this fight' queue), never simultaneous forced modals. The '5 strategic choices on screen' rule is meaningless if 4 unbudgeted interrupts can fire during one engagement. Make the interrupt budget part of the ship checklist.

RESOLVE THE AUTOMATION CONTRADICTION EXPLICITLY BY TIER: auto-hauling and auto-repeat-production (obviously-correct, no interesting decision) = fully automated, penalty-free, agreed. Convoy ROUTING and ESCORT = a one-time 'set the route + assign an escort' decision that then runs autonomously, with raids generating a deferrable alert — NOT live babysitting. That keeps convoy-cutting a real attack vector (the route is a standing commitment the enemy can punish) WITHOUT making convoy defense a per-second chore. Write down, per system, exactly which verb is manual and which is automated — the design currently hand-waves this and it's where the 'fast' claim will live or die.

PRESSURE-TEST 'FAST STELLARIS' AGAINST THE RIGHT NORTH STAR. Rise of Nations (already the stated star) actually proves this CAN work at real-time speed — but RoN succeeds because its strategic systems (borders, attrition, library research) are SLOW-CHANGING BACKGROUND STATE you set occasionally, not per-fight interrupts. The design drifts from RoN (background strategic state) toward CoH (high-decision-density DURING fights) and that drift is the danger. Re-anchor: strategic layer = low-frequency, set-between-engagements; tactical layer = the twitch fight, kept clean. If a system demands attention DURING a fight, it belongs in the tactical layer and must pass the twitch bar — or be cut.
critiques.detail:
VERDICT: fun-with-fixes — but the fixes are load-bearing, not cosmetic. The design is unusually self-aware (the decision-density pillar, the anti-stalemate ship checklists, the explicit 'add systems ≠ fun' framing, and the candid open-questions list are all genuinely strong, and rare). It has clearly anticipated the pacing-purist objection. My job is to show that anticipating it in PROSE is not the same as engineering around it, and several core mechanics quietly violate the very pillars that are supposed to protect the fast feel.

THE CENTRAL TENSION THE DESIGN ASSERTS AWAY: 'fast Stellaris' is not a contradiction in the abstract — Rise of Nations is the existence proof, and the design correctly names it. The contradiction is specific and mechanical: Stellaris-class DEPTH is tolerable in real time only if the strategic decisions are LOW-FREQUENCY and SELF-PACED (you choose when to engage them, usually between fights), as in RoN. This design repeatedly puts strategic decisions on the OPPONENT's tempo and INSIDE the fight: timed diplomacy toasts, saturation-driven defense micro, convoy raids, minor-faction races. Those are event-driven interrupts, and interrupts are the enemy of twitch flow because they seize the one scarce resource an RA player is spending on the battlefield — attention and cursor. The match timer is not the pacing risk; the ATTENTION budget is, and the design budgets on-screen choices (~5) while leaving event-driven interrupts completely unbudgeted.

WHERE THE DESIGN'S OWN PILLARS INDICT IT: Pillar 1 ('decision density, not management load') and Pillar 5 ('progressive disclosure keeps it fast') are the right instincts, but (a) disclosure only addresses onboarding, not the late-game where all layers co-exist during the biggest fights, and (b) the 'active defense as verbs not autopilot' system is, by a pacing purist's reading, MANAGEMENT LOAD wearing a decision-density costume — it adds a second simultaneous micro-front rather than enriching the existing one. The design even flags the smoking guns itself: open question #4 ('is even 3 stockpiles too much cognitive load in real-time combat?') and #6 (EMP-on-the-power-grid as a possible coin-flip swing) are admissions that the steady-state attention load is unvalidated.

WHAT'S ACTUALLY GOOD AND SHOULD SURVIVE: territory-is-economy is the single best pacing-positive idea here — it kills the deathball AND removes harvester micro AND makes map control legible, all without per-second load (CoH proves it). The era-gate spine (4 tiers, bounded snowball) is sound and on-genre. Saturation-vulnerable defense as a cost-exchange CONCEPT is excellent; only its DELIVERY (live multi-verb micro) is pacing-hostile. The 'automate the tedium' instinct is correct; it's just under-specified to the point of contradiction. The art-first sequencing and metric-gated playtesting discipline are exactly right and materially de-risk the whole program.

THE ONE-LINE FIX THESIS: push every strategic system toward 'set it between fights, it runs itself during fights, it generates at most one deferrable alert.' Keep the tactical fight as clean and autopilot-light on the DEFENSE side as RA's is. If a system insists on live attention during an engagement, it must pass the twitch bar or be cut — measured by a new first-class metric: camera/cursor time on your own army during contested fights. Get that one number right on the MVP (territory + 1 stockpile + dynamic relationships, nothing else) before adding a single further layer, and 'fast Stellaris' stops being an aspiration and becomes a measurable, defended property. Ship it broad before proving that, and the battlefield the user loves will quietly lose to the dashboard the design admires.

topConcerns: THE ONBOARDING DEFENSE IS VAPORWARE. The design's entire answer to new-player overload is 'progressive disclosure + the Codex doubles as a just-in-time tutorial.' I verified both load-bearing claims against the repo and both fail. (1) OpenRA ships ZERO tutorial infrastructure — no tutorial map in mods/ra/maps, no TutorialLogic in Widgets/Logic, no onboarding tooltips, no contextual hint system. The engine has literally never had to teach anyone anything. (2) The Codex it leans on is OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/Encyclopedia.cs — I read it: it is a passive static reference card (a Desc string, an Order int, a Category, a preview Scale). There is NO event hook, NO 'card pops the first time you mine a deposit,' NO trigger machinery. The 'just-in-time teacher' that minute-one onboarding depends on is software that does not exist and is nowhere in the ~5% engine-glue budget. The single most important new-player safety net in the entire design is asserted, not designed.

THE 'PROGRESSIVE DISCLOSURE' PROMISE COLLIDES WITH RTS REAL-TIME. Progressive disclosure works in turn-based 4X because the player has unlimited time to read each new panel when it appears. Here, the research button, doctrine perks, diplomacy radial, three stockpile counters, and food/water bar all 'reveal themselves as the match unlocks them' — i.e. mid-fight, on a clock, while the opponent is attacking. A new UI element appearing during combat is not gentle onboarding; it is an interruption demanding a decision the player has never made before, with no pause to absorb it (the design explicitly forbids Stellaris-style pause-to-think). You have built a 4X-depth surface and then scheduled its reveal for the exact moments the player has the least free attention.

THE WORKING-MEMORY BUDGET IS SELF-CONTRADICTED BY ITS OWN NUMBERS. The design claims a '~5 actionable choices on screen' ceiling and '1 number constantly + 3 occasionally + 2 bars' as 'under the working-memory ceiling.' Count what a mid-game player is actually tracking simultaneously: Credits + 3 strategic stockpiles + Power bar + Food/Water bar + interceptor magazine pips across multiple batteries + SAM dead-zone rings + convoy supply lines that can be cut + minor-faction loyalty scores + diplomatic pact expiry timers + era-up + doctrine perks + 1-2 upgrade forks + the classic RTS load (base, army, scouting, micro). That is not 5 choices; it is a dozen persistent state-trackers layered on top of an already-demanding RTS. The 'under the ceiling' claim is achieved only by counting the resource HUD in isolation and ignoring everything else competing for the same attention.

ASYMMETRY-BY-MATCHUP MULTIPLIES THE LEARNING CLIFF, NOT FLATTENS IT. The design treats 12 blocs each with a unique mechanic + unit + building as cheap variety. From a cognitive-load lens it is the opposite: to play competently a new player must learn THEIR faction's signature mechanic AND the 11 enemy signatures, because the whole design rests on 'attack the seam' (snipe USA's C2 node, flank the German Leopard, splash Iran's swarm, exploit the SAM dead zone). A new player does not know these seams exist, gets punished by them invisibly, and has no feedback loop explaining why they lost. That is the textbook bounce trigger: defeat without comprehensible cause. 132 directional matchup interactions is a pro-scene knowledge tax, not a new-player on-ramp.

THE IRREVERSIBLE DOCTRINE FORK IS ANALYSIS-PARALYSIS BY DESIGN. An early, permanent Economy/Military/Defense/Diplomacy choice shown 'up front' to a player who does not yet understand what diplomacy, EW, or strategic upkeep even do is a high-stakes decision made with zero information. New players freeze on irreversible choices precisely because they cannot evaluate them. Pairing 'irreversible' with 'minute-one player has never seen these systems' guarantees either paralysis or a regretted commit that sours the whole match — and the design's own openDesignQuestions admit the 'one best doctrine' trap is unsolved, meaning a new player's safe move is to copy a guide, which kills the choice entirely.
whatWouldFixIt: BUILD THE 'JUST-IN-TIME CODEX' AS A REAL, SCOPED ENGINEERING DELIVERABLE BEFORE CLAIMING IT AS THE ONBOARDING ANSWER. Add an event-triggered hint trait (fires on first-mine-of-resource, first-unlock, first-enemy-signature-seen) that surfaces a dismissable Codex card. This is genuinely new C# (notify hooks + a HintManager + a 'seen' set persisted per profile), not the free reuse the design implies. Until it exists and is playtested, treat onboarding as UNSOLVED, not solved. Also commission an actual interactive tutorial mission — OpenRA has Lua scripting and the map editor; there is no excuse for shipping a 4X-hybrid with no guided first hour.

STAGGER SYSTEM REVEALS BY MATCH, NOT BY MINUTE. Ship a 'campaign/skirmish ladder' where the first 2-3 matches a new player ever plays have diplomacy OFF, stockpiles at exactly 1, and doctrine locked — so they learn the core RTS loop to mastery FIRST, then each subsequent unlocked-by-progression match adds exactly one cross-coupled system. Reveal-within-a-match is too fast; reveal-across-matches respects how RTS players actually onboard (this is how StarCraft and AoE campaigns gate complexity).

MAKE THE DOCTRINE FORK REVERSIBLE-WITH-A-COST OR DEFER IT PAST ERA 1. An early irreversible identity choice is the single worst cognitive-load decision in the design. Either let players re-fork by paying a real credit/time penalty (so a mistake is recoverable, not match-ending) or push the fork to Era 2 after the player has seen the systems in action and can choose informedly. Preserve the 'big legible choice' fantasy without making it a blind irreversible gamble.

ADD A LOSS-REASON FEEDBACK LAYER so seam-based defeats are comprehensible. After a match, surface 'your C2 node was sniped at 8:14, collapsing your army buff' or 'your SAM had no SHORAD screen and was killed in its dead zone.' Without this, the matchup-knowledge tax is invisible and players bounce from inexplicable losses. This is cheap (you already track the events) and converts the depth from punishing to teaching.

HARD-CAP THE SIMULTANEOUS STATE-TRACKERS AND VALIDATE IN PLAYTEST, COUNTING EVERYTHING. Re-do the working-memory budget counting ALL persistent trackers (resources + magazines + rings + loyalty + pact timers + supply lines), not just the resource HUD. If the honest count exceeds ~7, cut. The design already proposes decision-density metric gates — add an explicit 'new-player 10-match retention' and 'time-to-first-comprehended-loss' gate, and ship the MVP (Credits + ONE stockpile + dynamic diplomacy, as the design itself proposes) and PROVE a newcomer can have fun in it before adding layer two. The MVP scoping instinct is correct; enforce it as a gate, not an aspiration.

PICK ONE PRIMARY CUSTOMER. The openDesignQuestions flag that diplomacy/minors are recommended OFF for ranked 1v1 — meaning the rich-hybrid mode and the lean-competitive mode are two different games with two different onboarding problems. Decide which player the onboarding optimizes for and design the new-player path for that one; trying to serve both doubles the teaching surface you already cannot afford.
critiques.detail:
VERDICT: risky — specifically on the cognitive-load/new-player axis. The design is unusually self-aware (it cites the Sid Meier filter, the onboarding-cliff killer, the working-memory ceiling, and even bakes anti-overload language into every pillar), and that earns it 'risky' rather than 'likely-not-fun.' But self-awareness in the prose is not the same as the problem being solved, and on inspection the load-bearing onboarding mechanisms are asserted rather than built.

The decisive finding is repo-verified. The design's whole answer to 'is this too much to learn at once?' is two mechanisms: progressive disclosure and a Codex-as-just-in-time-tutorial. I checked both. (1) OpenRA has NO tutorial system — no tutorial map under mods/ra/maps, no TutorialLogic class, no contextual tooltip/hint machinery anywhere in OpenRA.Mods.Common/Widgets/Logic. The engine has 45 widget-logic classes already (a non-trivial existing UI surface a newcomer must absorb) and none of them teach. (2) The Codex the design names as the teacher is Encyclopedia.cs — I read it and it is a static description card: a Fluent Desc string, an Order int, a Category heading, a preview scale. It has no event triggers, no 'pops when you first mine the deposit,' no notify hooks. The diegetic just-in-time teaching that the uiDirection section describes in loving detail is fiction relative to the actual code. So the design's single most important new-player safety net is, today, vaporware — and it is nowhere in the '~5% engine glue' budget, which is spent entirely on the diplomacy/research/defense sim traits.

Why this matters for the lens specifically: every other concern (the dozen simultaneous state-trackers, the 132-matchup seam-knowledge tax, the irreversible blind doctrine fork, the mid-combat reveal of brand-new UI) is survivable IF and ONLY IF there is a strong teaching layer absorbing the load. The design knows this — that is why it leans so hard on the Codex. Remove the (nonexistent) teaching layer and the cognitive load lands raw on a player who, in an RTS, has no pause button to think. The progressive-disclosure idea is sound in turn-based 4X and actively dangerous in real-time: revealing a new system mid-match means revealing it at the moment the player has the least spare attention.

Is the complexity depth or busywork? Genuinely mixed. The cross-coupling thesis (few systems feeding each other) is the right north star and the territory-is-economy / supply-cutting / saturation-valve mechanics are real depth that does kill the deathball. That is the fun core, and the MVP the design itself proposes (Credits + one stockpile + dynamic diplomacy) could be genuinely good. But the 12-bloc asymmetry, three stockpiles, food/water meter, and live diplomacy with minors are additive load stacked on top, and the design's own openDesignQuestions admit the most balance- and load-sensitive numbers (era-up timing, pact tuning, doctrine viability, whether even 3 stockpiles is too much) are ALL unvalidated hypotheses. That is honest, but it means the 'depth not load' claim is currently faith, not evidence.

The path is clear and the design already half-knows it: ship the MVP, build the Codex-trigger and a real tutorial mission as actual engineering deliverables (not assumed-free reuse), stagger system reveals across matches rather than within them, make the doctrine fork recoverable, and add a loss-reason feedback layer so seam-defeats teach instead of just punishing. Prove a newcomer has fun and can explain why they lost in the one-system MVP before adding layer two. Do that and this moves to fun-with-fixes. Ship the full 12-bloc, 3-stockpile, live-diplomacy hybrid with a static encyclopedia and no tutorial, and new players will bounce off the onboarding cliff the design correctly names but does not actually bridge.

Key repo anchors for whoever acts on this: /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/Encyclopedia.cs (the static card that is NOT a tutorial), /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/OpenRA.Mods.Common/Widgets/Logic/EncyclopediaLogic.cs, and the absence to note: no tutorial map in /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/mods/ra/maps and no TutorialLogic in /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/OpenRA.Mods.Common/Widgets/Logic/.

topConcerns: COMBINATORIAL BALANCE IS UNWINNABLE AT SHIP SCOPE. 12 factions x 4 irreversible doctrines x 3 eras x 'pick N of M' era-upgrade forks x ON/OFF diplomacy is not 12 matchups, it is hundreds of effectively-distinct strategic archetypes whose pairings must each be non-degenerate. StarCraft 2 ships 3 factions and Blizzard still patches it for a decade; this design proposes ~4x the asymmetry surface with a solo/small team. The doctrine fork multiplies the country axis it claims to express. 'Balanced by role not power tier' is an aspiration, not a mechanism, and the design provides no per-matchup balancing methodology beyond 'playtest gates.' This is the single most likely point of failure.

ON/OFF DIPLOMACY FORKS THE GAME INTO TWO UNBALANCEABLE PRODUCTS. The design itself admits ranked 1v1 should run diplomacy OFF. That means every faction must be balanced TWICE: once in a lean kinetic game and once in a minor-faction/pact game. A faction whose entire identity is a unique BUILDING that buffs diplomacy/intel (the design explicitly puts UK Maritime Ops Centre, the Diplomacy-Intel doctrine, etc. in this space) is structurally weaker or broken in the OFF mode that the competitive scene will actually adopt. You cannot tune one knob to fix both modes simultaneously.

DIPLOMACY-AS-KINGMAKING DESTROYS COMPETITIVE INTEGRITY IN FFA. Live binding alliances with a Vassal/Protectorate comeback mechanic means the outcome of a 4+ player match is decided by who two humans agree to gang, not by play skill. The 3-5s telegraphed betrayal window is itself an exploit: it converts alliances into a guaranteed free-alpha-strike timing (ally, position inside their base under shared-control, declare, fire after grace) that is strictly better than honest war. Kingmaking and the alpha-strike exploit are the two classic reasons RTS ladders ban FFA from ranked entirely.

SNOWBALL VECTORS ARE STACKED, NOT BOUNDED. The design layers THREE compounding lead-amplifiers and waves them off individually: (a) era advantage ('player one era ahead near-unbeatable', their words), (b) veterancy (GainsExperience exists and is assumed on, so the winning army gets permanently better), (c) territory-IS-economy (whoever holds more map both out-produces AND out-techs AND out-diplomaces because deposits gate doctrine). CoH's territory model snowballs notoriously hard for exactly this reason. The listed brakes (4 capped eras, upkeep decay, Vassal comeback) are weak against three multiplicative sources; the comeback mechanic is itself a kingmaking lever. 20-40 min matches will frequently be decided by minute 10 with 25 minutes of non-interactive mop-up.

ACTIVE DEFENSE + EW POWER-COUPLING INVITES BOTH STALEMATE AND COIN-FLIP. Two failure modes pull opposite directions and both are live. Stalemate: a defensive-doctrine faction (Israel APS/Iron-Dome, China Integrated Defense Grid, Japan Aegis) stacking layered AD on a chokepoint, fed by upkeep from held territory, can make assault permanently cost-inefficient on small/positional maps -- 'saturation-beatable' assumes the attacker can out-produce the magazine, but a turtle with superior economy refills faster than you drain. Coin-flip: the design's own open question admits tying the whole AD/EW net to the power grid makes one EMP raid swing defense from oppressive to useless. Competitive players will find whichever pole is stronger and live there.

DOMINANT-STRATEGY RISK IS HIGH AND UNDER-DEFENDED. 'Tech competes with the same credit pool as units' makes greed punishable -- which historically means the dominant ladder line becomes the all-in rush that punishes any teching/expanding/diplo-investing opponent before payoff (cf. every economy-vs-army RTS converging on timing pushes). The 'decision-density metrics as ship gates' are a process aspiration, not a design solution; they can detect a dominant strategy but the design names no structural answer for when (not if) the rush dominates the rich-systems line.
whatWouldFixIt: SHRINK THE COMPETITIVE CORE HARD, sell the rest as a separate mode. Ship ranked 1v1 with 3-4 factions, ONE strategic stockpile, NO irreversible doctrine fork (make doctrine a per-match pick from 2, not 4, or cut it for v1), diplomacy OFF, and freeze that as the balance product. Treat 12-faction + diplomacy + minors as a distinct 'Skirmish/FFA' mode with its own (looser, explicitly-not-esports) balance bar. Stop trying to make one ruleset serve both. This directly answers concerns 1 and 2 and is consistent with the design's own Phase-1 instinct -- just make the small scope the SHIPPING competitive scope, not a stepping stone.

MAKE DIPLOMACY NON-BINDING ON THE SIM in competitive contexts. Replace shared-CONTROL alliances with vision-and-economy-only pacts (no units inside an ally's base, no shared command), which kills the alpha-strike exploit. Gate any war-declaration with a hard cooldown AND a sim-enforced no-fire-on-former-ally window long enough that betrayal is a tempo LOSS, not a free alpha strike. For FFA, cap simultaneous allies at 1 and make the Vassal comeback give the vassal economy/vision, never controllable military -- so it is a survival lifeline, not a kingmaking transfer.

REPLACE MULTIPLICATIVE SNOWBALL WITH BOUNDED/RUBBER-BANDED LEADS. Make veterancy decay or cap low in competitive mode (or off). Make era advantage a CEILING-raise with strong cross-era counters that are CHEAP and tier-1-buildable (the design names MANPADS-kills-Near-Future-asset -- commit to that as a hard rule, costed so the behind player can always punish over-extension). Add diminishing returns on territory income past N sectors so map control helps but does not compound into auto-win. Make deposit upkeep bite the LEADER hardest (more doctrines active = more convoy exposure), turning a lead into a defensive liability rather than a flywheel.

DECOUPLE DEFENSE FROM A SINGLE POWER SPOF and price the turtle out structurally. Give core AD a battery-backup so EMP degrades-gracefully (caps the coin-flip), but make every static AD layer cost ONGOING strategic-stockpile upkeep that scales superlinearly with coverage area, so a wall-of-domes turtle starves its own tech -- expanding-beats-sitting must be enforced by the cost curve, not hoped for in playtest. Add a mandatory minimum-range/screen dependency (already designed for theater SAM) to EVERY static layer so pure static defense is impossible without mobile support that can be baited out.

DEFINE THE ANTI-RUSH FLOOR EXPLICITLY, don't delegate it to playtest gates. Guarantee a survivable opening: a cheap, always-available tier-1 defensive option per faction that makes the all-in coin-flip unfavorable, plus an era/tech cost curve tuned so the FIRST tech investment pays back before a standard timing push lands. State the target win-rate spread for 'greedy tech' vs 'all-in' openings as a numeric ship criterion (e.g. neither strategy >55% across the matchup matrix) rather than 'no-dominant-strategy lens in playtest.'

ADD A REAL BALANCE METHODOLOGY, not just alarms. Commit to a matchup-matrix process: a frozen reference faction, automated AI mirror/cross self-play to surface degenerate lines cheaply before human playtest, and a public PTR cadence. Sequence asymmetry LAST: ship factions as near-mirrors with one signature unit each, prove the economic/territory loop is fun symmetric, THEN layer signature mechanics one faction at a time behind the matrix. The doctrine fork should be the last thing added, because it is the largest multiplier on the matrix you must keep non-degenerate.
critiques.detail:
I verified the engine claims in-repo because the design's feasibility argument is load-bearing, and they largely hold: AlliedPlayersMask/EnemyPlayersMask are mutable LongBitSet fields set once in CreateMapPlayers.SetupPlayerMasks (OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/World/CreateMapPlayers.cs:142) and never mutated, so the ~250 LOC DiplomacyManager claim is plausible; World.SharedRandom is a seeded MersenneTwister (OpenRA.Game/World.cs:199) so synced RNG for interception is available; GainsExperience, RegionProximityCapturable, ProductionQueue, PlayerResources, and JamsMissiles all exist as claimed. So the engineering risk really is ~70% YAML as stated. THAT IS THE PROBLEM, not the reassurance the design treats it as: when the engine is cheap, the entire project risk collapses onto BALANCE and CONTENT, which are exactly the two things this design is most optimistic and least concrete about.

Through the competitive/balance lens, the design is a fun SKIRMISH game wearing an esports aspiration it cannot support at the stated scope. The good news first, honestly: the core anti-deathball thesis (territory-is-economy + hard counters + saturation-vulnerable defense + opportunity-cost tech) is genuinely sound and is the strongest part -- these are real, proven levers (CoH, SC2) and they correctly attack the 'mass-and-A-move' loop. If the project shipped JUST that, symmetric or near-symmetric, with 3-4 factions and no diplomacy, it would likely be fun and balanceable.

But the lens question was: is THIS balanceable and esports-viable? No, as scoped. Three structural reasons compound. (1) The asymmetry surface is mis-counted. The design frames it as '12 matchups, not numbers,' but the real matrix is 12 factions x 4 irreversible doctrines x era-upgrade forks -- the doctrine fork the design adds to EXPRESS faction identity is simultaneously the largest MULTIPLIER on the balance matrix it must keep non-degenerate. (2) The diplomacy ON/OFF toggle is presented as a clean lobby option but is actually a fork into two products requiring two independent balance passes, and several faction identities (anything in the Diplomacy-Intel doctrine, the UK/intel building) are structurally mode-dependent. (3) Every named snowball brake is weak against the fact that THREE lead-amplifiers (era, veterancy, territory-gated tech-AND-economy-AND-diplomacy) all point the same direction; the design even concedes 'one era ahead = near-unbeatable' as an open question and then proposes a comeback mechanic (Vassal) that is itself a kingmaking lever in any non-1v1 game.

The 1v1 diplomacy question specifically: it is NOT pointless thanks to the minor-faction race -- that is a legitimately clever way to make a third party to fight over in a 1v1, and it is the design's best original idea. But it is also the most art-blocked (the design's own open question flags that exciting minor rewards need sprites that won't exist at launch, leaving art-free payloads that 'blunt the race fantasy'), so the one thing that justifies diplomacy in 1v1 is the thing most likely to ship hollow. And the moment you leave 1v1, binding alliances + telegraphed betrayal create kingmaking and a free-alpha-strike exploit that are the textbook reasons ladders ban FFA.

Net: the path to viable is to stop treating the small scope as Phase 1 and treat it as THE competitive product -- lean 1v1, 3-4 factions, one stockpile, no irreversible fork, diplomacy off -- freeze and balance that to an explicit numeric matchup-spread criterion, and sell the 12-faction/diplomacy/minors vision as an explicitly-not-esports rich skirmish mode. The design has the right instincts (Phase 1 already isolates the loop; decision-density gates show balance awareness) but currently lets the ambitious mode write checks the competitive mode has to cash. Verdict fun-with-fixes: the core loop is fun and the engine is real, but esports-viability and the full asymmetric/diplomatic vision are not simultaneously achievable, and the fixes are mostly about cutting and forking scope rather than adding cleverness.

topConcerns: The design has a load-bearing AI dependency it never addresses. Diplomacy/city-states are pitched as the thing that 'makes the strategic layer live even in 1v1 and skirmish-vs-AI' — but OpenRA's bot is ~6,400 lines of hand-authored, archetype-locked scripting (mods/ra/rules/ai.yaml defines fixed rush/normal/turtle/naval bots). There is NO relationship-mutation code, NO opinion model for the bot-as-actor, and the only diplomacy the design specs for AI is the MINOR faction's acceptance score — i.e. how an NPC reacts to YOU, not how the bot plays diplomacy against you. In skirmish, the human races an opponent that will never bid on, betray over, or even contest a minor. The 'third party to fight over' becomes a free pickup for the human, and the headline 1v1-skirmish justification for the entire diplomacy system collapses.

Asymmetric factions break the bot, and the design admits the mechanism without seeing the consequence. The current AI composes armies from a STATIC ratio dict (UnitBuilderBotModule.UnitsToBuild) and buildings from fixed BuildingFractions — it cannot reason about counters at all. The design's own anti-spam pillar requires that 'a pure top-tier stack is strictly cost-inefficient vs a screened mixed force' and that each signature unit has an exploitable seam (snipe USA's C2 node, flank the Leopard, splash Iran's swarm). A fixed-ratio bot cannot screen its SAM's dead zone, cannot protect its C2 aura node, cannot saturate an interceptor magazine on purpose, and cannot exploit any of those seams on offense. Every faction's 'identity' is invisible to the AI both as user and opponent — meaning 12 asymmetric blocs require up to 12 hand-tuned bot profiles times 4 archetypes, and even then the bot plays each as a generic blob.

The two cross-coupled systems the design is proudest of are exactly the two the scripted AI is worst at. (a) RESEARCH: teching draws the SAME credit pool as units and forks irreversibly into a doctrine — this is a genuine economic-tradeoff and timing decision. The existing bot has no opportunity-cost reasoning; it follows fixed BuildingDelays/UnitDelays timers. A bot that techs on a hardcoded timer will get rushed while army-light (the design's own open question #2) or will tech into a doctrine that hard-loses the on-map counter-triangle it can't perceive. (b) DEFENSE-as-verbs: the design explicitly reframes defense as '2-4 live decisions during an assault' (allocate interceptors, fire counter-battery, jam-burst, reposition SHORAD). Live micro-decisions under saturation pressure are the single hardest thing for a finite-state bot. Against the AI, 'active defense' degrades to autopilot turrets; the human's defense skill has no AI opponent to test it.

Solo play risks being theoretically deep but practically hollow, because the depth lives in the interactions the AI can't engage. The design's thesis is 'depth from a few cross-coupling systems,' but ALL the cross-couplings (economy gates research, research reshapes diplomacy leverage, diplomacy reshapes the contested map) are loops the bot neither initiates nor responds to. A human will quickly learn the bot never cuts your convoy, never bids on minors, never re-forks doctrine in response to your composition, and never repositions defense under a saturation push. The skirmish-vs-AI experience reduces to 'beat a static timer-bot that masses a fixed army' — i.e. the exact shallow 'mass-and-A-move' loop the design claims to have structurally killed, just with more UI panels the bot ignores. For an engine whose single-player IS skirmish + scripted missions, that is the primary customer being underserved.

Scope: the AI work is invisible in the build plan, which is itself the failure mode the design names ('the realistic failure is unfinished design'). The detail section budgets the new C# as diplomacy order (~250 LOC), ResearchQueue, strategic-resource counter, PointDefense, Food meter — and zero lines for bot modules to USE any of them. A credible AI for this design needs new bot modules for relationship decisions, convoy raiding/escorting, deposit contesting, era/doctrine selection with counter-awareness, strategic-resource upkeep management, and per-shot interceptor allocation — plausibly more new AI C# than the entire rest of the feature set combined, none of it scoped. Phase 1's 'no-dominant-strategy playtest gate' also implicitly assumes opponents that punish dominant strategies; against the stock bot, almost any greedy line passes, so the gate gives false-positive 'fun' signals.
whatWouldFixIt: Make every new system DEGRADE GRACEFULLY to a competent fixed policy, and spec that policy as a first-class deliverable per system. For diplomacy: give the bot a small deterministic relationship policy (bid on the nearest minor up to a budget tied to its credit lead; accept defensive pacts when behind; break NAPs only when it can win the resulting fight) — even a crude bot that CONTESTS minors restores the 1v1 'race' fantasy. Budget this as real C# bot modules, not an afterthought, and add it to the Phase-1 scope alongside the diplomacy order.

Tie the bot's composition and tech choices to faction tags and a coarse scouting signal so asymmetry is at least legible. Extend UnitBuilderBotModule with counter-aware overrides keyed off 'I have seen enemy build X' (the design already promises 'scouting economy = scouting tech'). Give each of the 6 launch blocs a hand-authored bot profile that at minimum protects its signature enabler building and screens its signature unit's named weakness. Ship 6 factions precisely so 6 bot profiles is tractable — don't broaden to 12 until the bot proves it can play the seam.

Convert the 'live defense verbs' into AI-friendly automatable policies with a visible skill ceiling for humans only. Let interceptor allocation, counter-battery, and SHORAD repositioning run as a sensible default policy (the design already commits to 'automate-the-tedium'); the human's edge is overriding it better, while the bot uses the default. This keeps defense functional on the AI side without requiring per-assault micro the scripted bot can't do, and avoids the autopilot-turret feel by making the DEFAULT genuinely decent.

Add a single explicit 'AI feasibility' gate to each Phase before its playtest gate: a system ships only if the stock bot can both USE it at a baseline and not be trivially exploited through it. Run dominant-strategy playtests against (a) the bot AND (b) a human sparring partner — if a line beats the bot but loses to a human, that's a bot gap to log, not a balanced system. This catches the false-positive 'fun' signal before art money is spent.

Reframe and budget single-player honestly: decide whether the primary solo experience is skirmish-vs-bot or scripted Lua missions. If missions, lean in — the design's scripted-event hooks and Codex-as-tutorial are strong, and Lua-authored opponents can FAKE diplomacy/convoy-cutting/doctrine-switching believably without a general AI. A mission campaign where scripted factions betray you, cut your supply lines, and tech-switch on triggers delivers the Stellaris-envelopment fantasy in solo far more reliably than asking the modular bot to improvise it. Make that the Phase-1 solo proof, and treat free-skirmish AI as a later, separately-scoped problem.

Add an open design question that the doc is conspicuously missing: 'Can the scripted bot play, and not be exploited through, each cross-coupled system — and if not, does that system get a lobby default-off like ranked 1v1?' The design already gates diplomacy On/Off for the ladder; the same toggle logic should be applied per-system for skirmish based on AI readiness, so solo players aren't handed systems their opponent provably ignores.
critiques.detail:
EVIDENCE FROM THE REPO (why this is not speculation): OpenRA's AI is the ModularBot, assembled from ~6,400 LOC of bot modules under OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/BotModules/. Its decision-making is (1) static composition — UnitBuilderBotModule reads a fixed UnitsToBuild ratio dictionary and UnitDelays timers; BaseBuilderBotModule reads fixed BuildingFractions/BuildingLimits/BuildingDelays; (2) fuzzy attack-or-flee — AttackOrFleeFuzzy.cs is a hand-written rule table over OwnHealth/EnemyHealth/RelativeAttackPower/RelativeSpeed; (3) support-power 'attractiveness' heuristics — SupportPowerBotModule picks a random above-average-attractiveness target. Config lives per-mod in YAML (mods/ra/rules/ai.yaml) as four fixed archetypes: rush/normal/turtle/naval. A grep for diplomacy/research/doctrine/era/stockpile/convoy/minor across all bot modules returns NOTHING. The bot has no API to mutate relationships (the design itself notes masks are set ONCE in CreateMapPlayers.SetupPlayerMasks and never change), no opportunity-cost economic model, and no counter-composition reasoning.

WHY THIS LENS IS DAMNING FOR THIS PARTICULAR DESIGN: the design's entire fun-thesis is 'depth from cross-coupling, not from parallel meters.' That is a great thesis for a HUMAN-vs-HUMAN game. But OpenRA's shipped single-player is skirmish-vs-bot plus Lua missions, and every cross-coupling the design relies on requires an opponent that participates in it. The diplomacy system is explicitly justified by 'makes the strategic layer live even in 1v1 and skirmish-vs-AI' — yet the only AI logic specced is the MINOR faction's integer opinion of the human. The bot-as-player gets nothing. So in skirmish: the human collects minors uncontested, the bot never cuts the human's convoy (the design's marquee 'economic warfare attack vector'), the bot techs on a hardcoded timer into a doctrine it can't match to the human's composition, and the bot's 'active layered defense' runs as dumb turrets because per-assault interceptor allocation is precisely what a finite-state machine cannot do well. The four headline systems all degrade to scenery on the AI side.

THE STRUCTURAL TRAP: the design markets itself as killing the 'mass the best unit and A-move' loop. Against the stock bot, it does the opposite — because the bot CAN ONLY mass a fixed army and A-move, the human faces exactly that shallow opponent while being told the game is deep. Worse, the design's own quality gate ('a system ships only if it passes the no-dominant-strategy lens in playtest') will return false positives if those playtests are run against the bot: almost any greedy line beats a timer-bot, so 'no dominant strategy found' would really mean 'the bot is too weak to punish anything.' Art money then gets committed on a fun signal that was an AI artifact.

WHAT IS GENUINELY SALVAGEABLE (the path, not just the wound): none of this means solo is doomed — it means the design must stop treating AI as free. Two credible routes. (A) Graceful-degradation policies: every system must have a competent FIXED default the bot can run (contest the nearest minor on a budget; raid/escort convoys with existing squad logic; tech on a counter-triggered rather than pure-timer basis; auto-allocate interceptors). This is real, unscoped C# — plausibly comparable in size to the rest of the new code — and belongs in Phase 1, not deferred. (B) Lean the solo proof on Lua scripted missions instead of free skirmish. The engine's Lua + scripted-event hooks can FAKE believable diplomacy, betrayal, supply-cutting, and doctrine-switching on triggers without a general AI, and the Codex-as-tutorial is genuinely well-conceived for guided onboarding. A campaign delivers the 'Stellaris envelopment' fantasy in solo far more reliably than the modular bot improvising it. The design should pick one of these as the Phase-1 single-player deliverable and add the missing open question — 'can the bot play, and not be exploited through, each system; if not, default it off in skirmish like ranked 1v1' — to the eight it already lists. The omission of any AI open question in a doc this thorough is itself the tell that single-player was not designed, only assumed.

NET: the systems are well-reasoned for competitive multiplayer and the engine-feasibility homework is solid, but the single-player/AI story is unwritten, and the doc leans on skirmish-vs-AI to justify the most expensive new system (diplomacy) while shipping no bot capable of playing it. Fixable with explicit AI-policy scoping and an honest choice of solo proof — hence 'risky,' not 'likely-not-fun.' But shipped as-written, solo play would be theoretically deep and practically hollow.

topConcerns: MULTI-YEAR TOTAL CONVERSION DISGUISED AS A MOD. The document concedes 'this is effectively a new game on an existing engine' and then proposes shipping it anyway. Count the bespoke deliverables: 12 blocs x (1 hero unit + 1 unique building) at 32-facing Blender-rendered+team-color-masked+indexed sprites = 24 hero assets minimum, PLUS a full SHARED modern base set (the design hand-waves 'one shared base set reused by all' but a contemporary-military RTS needs ~15-20 base unit types + ~15 buildings + terrain, every one of them new art because nothing in RA/CnC looks modern). I confirmed in-repo that RA's infantry sequence file alone defines 134 facing/animation entries and the mod ships 104+ SHPs for ONE faction's incidental art. A 'shared base set' for a playable contemporary RTS is realistically 150-250 new sprite sequences before a single hero unit. The 'HD-Pixel diorama' pipeline (Blender model -> 32-angle turntable -> downscale -> index -> team-color mask pass -> readability sign-off at combat zoom) is 1-3 days of skilled work PER unit even when the pipeline is dialed in, and it isn't dialed in yet. That is the entire scope-killer and the design knows it but buries it as 'the true cost ceiling' rather than letting it set the schedule.

FOUR NEW CROSS-COUPLED SYSTEMS IS THREE TOO MANY FOR A FIRST SHIP, AND THE CROSS-COUPLING IS A LIABILITY, NOT AN ASSET, DURING DEVELOPMENT. The design's headline virtue (economy gates research gates diplomacy reshapes map) is exactly what makes it unshippable incrementally: cross-coupled systems cannot be balanced in isolation, so you cannot prove territory-economy is fun until research exists, can't prove research until doctrines exist, can't prove doctrines until you have >1 faction, can't prove factions without the art. The openDesignQuestions section itself lists FIVE separate 'only-findable-in-playtest' tuning unknowns (pact duration, era-up timing, doctrine balance, stockpile count, EMP swinginess) that ALL entangle with each other. That is a combinatorial balancing nightmare for a solo/tiny team, and every one of those knobs can independently sink fun.

THE DETERMINISM TAX ON THE NEW C# IS UNDERSTATED AND CONCENTRATED IN THE RISKIEST TRAIT. The '~250 LOC' DiplomacyManager mutates AlliedPlayersMask/EnemyPlayersMask, which the design itself notes the engine sets ONCE at init and never changes - meaning AutoTarget, Locomotor pathing, and shroud all read state that has never been mutated mid-game. Making that mutable mid-match via synced orders is not 250 lines of mechanical work; it is a new class of desync and edge-case surface (a unit mid-attack-order when relationship flips, shroud recompute cost, frozen-actor layers, cached IResolveOrder targeting). PointDefense rolling per-projectile intercept chance every tick via synced RNG, the convoy/supply sim, and territory ownership ALL run inside world.Tick() and ALL must be perfectly integer/synced. Desyncs are the #1 subtle-bug class in this engine; the design treats determinism as a checklist item when it's the dominant ongoing cost.

THE 'SMALLEST VERTICAL SLICE THAT PROVES FUN' IS NEVER ACTUALLY NAMED - THE PHASING IS STILL TOO BIG. Phase 1 as written is 'territory-economy + 1 stockpile + dynamic diplomacy order, 2-3 blocs.' That is still THREE interacting systems plus multi-faction asymmetry plus a brand-new mutable-relationship engine feature before you learn ANYTHING about whether the core thesis is fun. The thesis is 'territory-is-economy kills the deathball and is more fun than the harvester loop.' That single claim can and should be tested with ZERO new factions, ZERO diplomacy, ZERO research, ZERO new art - just RA units with a territory-capture income mechanic. The design buried its own cheapest experiment.

FACTION-BY-STRATEGIC-USE IS AN UNPROVEN BALANCE BET AT 12X SCALE, AND THE 'PHASE 2 SIX' WILL NEVER SHIP. Asymmetry-by-role with paired strength/weakness is the hardest balance problem in RTS (StarCraft does it with THREE factions and a full-time balance team across a decade). The design proposes 12, each with a unique mechanic + unit + building, then admits the right first ship 'is even smaller than 6.' Realistic outcome: 3-4 blocs get balanced and the back half becomes permanent vaporware, leaving an asymmetric roster that's lopsided - the worst state for a competitive RTS.

REAL-COUNTRY MILITARY THEMING IS A SHIPPING/DISTRIBUTION RISK THE SCOPE CANNOT ABSORB. 'Lightly-fictionalized real blocs' fighting with named real systems (BrahMos, Bayraktar, Shahed, Patriot-vs-Shahed economics, Iron Dome) plus a Codex teaching 'real military tech' invites storefront content-policy friction, regional bans, and community blowback that a solo dev cannot triage. The flavor-neutral toggle is sound but doubles UI/naming/asset-string work (two complete naming sets, two Codex copies) - a real cost line the budget never accounts for.
whatWouldFixIt: NAME THE ZERO-ART VERTICAL SLICE EXPLICITLY AND SHIP IT BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE. Slice 0: stock RA mod + ONE new mechanic - capturable territory sectors that pay income, replacing (not augmenting) the harvester. No new factions, no diplomacy, no research, no stockpiles, no art. One question only: 'does holding-and-cutting ground feel better than mass-and-A-move?' If that single change isn't fun with reskinned existing units, the entire thesis is dead and you've spent days, not years. Every later system is conditional on this passing.

SERIALIZE THE SYSTEMS HARD; FORBID PARALLEL DEVELOPMENT. Ship territory-economy ALONE and balance it. Only then add the strategic-stockpile gate (still art-free, gating an EXISTING RA superweapon as a stand-in). Only then add ONE doctrine fork. Diplomacy/minors comes dead last because it is the riskiest new C# (mutable masks) AND the least core to the deathball thesis. Treat each as independently shippable and independently fun-gated, even though they will eventually couple.

PROTOTYPE THE MUTABLE-MASK DIPLOMACY FEATURE AS A STANDALONE DETERMINISM SPIKE FIRST, in an existing mod with two AI players toggling Ally/Enemy mid-match on a timer, and run it through the sync-hash/replay validation under combat load BEFORE designing any of the 7 agreements or UI. Budget it as a multi-week engine task, not 250 lines. If mid-match mask mutation can't be made desync-clean cheaply, cut live diplomacy entirely and keep static lobby-set relationships - the rest of the design survives without it.

CAP THE FIRST PLAYABLE AT 3 BLOCS THAT SPAN THE DESIGN SPACE (one elite-expensive, one cheap-swarm, one defensive-denial), and make them DIFFER ONLY IN YAML STATS + ONE shared-base reskin - defer all bespoke hero sprites until those 3 are proven balanced and fun. The 12-bloc roster lives in the Codex/design doc as aspiration, gated behind a green light that, realistically, may never come - and the game must be complete and good at 3.

MAKE THE ART PIPELINE THROUGHPUT THE MASTER SCHEDULE VARIABLE. Before committing, render ONE unit fully through Blender->32-facing->team-color->in-engine->combat-zoom-readability-signoff and MEASURE the wall-clock. Multiply by the real base-set count (~150-250 sequences) to get an honest timeline. If one artist can't sustain the throughput, the project is multi-year by arithmetic - decide that with eyes open rather than discovering it in year two. Consider shipping the systems on a reskinned/recolored existing art set as a legitimate v1 and treating bespoke HD art as DLC-grade post-launch work.

DEFAULT TO FLAVOR-NEUTRAL FICTIONAL BLOCS AS THE PRIMARY ART/STRING SET (not a toggle bolted on later), and make real-country flavor the optional skin. This removes a content-policy risk, halves the worst-case localization/Codex duplication (one canonical naming set), and lets the educational Codex stay as opt-in lore rather than a load-bearing, scrutinized feature.

REPLACE THE FIVE OPEN TUNING UNKNOWNS WITH KILL-SWITCH DEFAULTS. For each entangled knob (era-up timing, pact duration, doctrine parity, stockpile count, EMP swing), pre-commit a 'if this isn't tunable to fun in N playtests, this system gets cut to a simpler fallback' rule. The design already has decision-density metric gates - apply them as CUT gates, not just ship gates, so the scope can actually shrink under pressure instead of only growing.
critiques.detail:
VERDICT RATIONALE (fun-with-fixes, leaning risky): The CORE thesis - territory-is-economy kills the deathball - is genuinely fun and is the one part defensible on its own. Everything bolted onto it (4 cross-coupled systems, 12 asymmetric real-world blocs, a bespoke HD sprite pipeline, a UI overhaul, an educational Codex, live mutable diplomacy) is what turns a tight, provable RTS mod into a multi-year total conversion that, realistically, never finishes. The design document is unusually self-aware - it flags the art ceiling, the scope risk, the determinism risk, and the tuning unknowns - but self-awareness is not scope control. It diagnoses every problem and then proposes to ship all of it anyway, just 'phased.'

VERIFIED IN-REPO: (1) The engine plumbing claims are largely TRUE - ProductionQueue (813 LOC) is a real template for ResearchQueue, JamsMissiles/AmmoPool exist, PlayerResources (264 LOC) is cloneable, the Encyclopedia widget exists. So the '70% data-only' claim is directionally credible FOR THE SYSTEMS. (2) The resource index is a `byte` in ResourceLayer.cs, so the '~7 tile resources' constraint is actually a non-issue (256 available) - a rare case where the design UNDERSELLS the engine. (3) The deal-killer is unchanged: RA's infantry sequences alone define 134 facing/animation entries and one faction ships 104+ SHPs of incidental art. A playable CONTEMPORARY base set is new art top to bottom, because nothing in the classic mods reads as modern military. The 'shared base set reused by palette swap' line is doing enormous unexamined work - palette swaps differentiate FACTIONS of the same unit, they do not conjure the 15-20 modern base unit types and 15 buildings that don't exist yet.

WHAT GETS CUT, REALISTICALLY (the honest forecast): live diplomacy + minors (riskiest C#, least core - first to go), blocs 7-12 (never balanced), 2 of 3 strategic stockpiles, the full layered-AD ladder collapses to 1-2 tiers, the UI overhaul shrinks to 'keep the sidebar, add a few counters,' and bespoke hero art arrives for 3-4 factions at most. If the team plans for that endgame DELIBERATELY - 3 blocs, territory-economy + one gated tech tier, reskinned art, flavor-neutral names - it is a shippable, genuinely novel, fun OpenRA mod in a realistic timeframe. If they try to ship the document as written, the failure mode is the one the doc itself names: 'unfinished design, not bad design.' The path to fun is to let the art-pipeline throughput and the determinism spike set the schedule, name and ship the zero-art territory slice FIRST, and treat every system after it as independently cut-able. The fun is real; the scope is the enemy.

Key files for the implementing team (absolute): /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/OpenRA.Game/Player.cs (mask state that must become mutable - the determinism spike target), /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/World/ResourceLayer.cs (byte index - more headroom than the design assumed), /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/OpenRA.Mods.Common/Traits/Player/ProductionQueue.cs (ResearchQueue template, confirmed viable), /Users/ashishnaik/Projects/openra/mods/ra/sequences/infantry.yaml (134-entry facing scale - the art-cost reality check).

roadmap.overallFunVerdict: CONDITIONAL GO — but only for a radically descoped first ship. GREEN-LIGHT the core thesis (territory-is-economy on a contemporary reskin); RED-LIGHT the document as written (12 blocs + 4 cross-coupled systems + live diplomacy + bespoke HD art is a multi-year total conversion mislabeled as a mod). The fun is real and locatable; the scope is the enemy and will kill this if not cut now.
roadmap.verdictRationale:
Synthesizing the five lenses rather than averaging them: the panel split 2 "fun-with-fixes" / 2 "risky" / 1 "fun-with-fixes", but every lens — including the optimistic ones — converges on the SAME load-bearing finding, which is decisive. That convergence is the signal. The single fun idea all five lenses independently endorse is TERRITORY-IS-ECONOMY: it kills the deathball, removes harvester micro, makes the map legible, and is proven (CoH). It is the only part defensible on its own and it needs zero new art. Everything bolted onto it is where the panel's fire concentrates, and the fires overlap in a damning pattern:

(1) The pacing purist and the cognitive-load lens make the same point from two directions — the design budgets ON-SCREEN choices (~5) but leaves EVENT-DRIVEN INTERRUPTS (diplomacy toasts with countdown rings, convoy raids, minor flips, AD saturation) completely unbudgeted, and those interrupts arrive mid-fight on the OPPONENT's tempo. "Fast Stellaris" works in Rise of Nations only because RoN's strategic layer is low-frequency background state you set BETWEEN fights; this design drifts toward CoH-style high-decision-density DURING fights. That drift is the core risk, and it is mechanical, not cosmetic.

(2) The cognitive-load and single-player/AI lenses both found that the design's load-bearing safety nets are VAPORWARE, repo-verified: the Codex (Encyclopedia.cs, 47 lines) is a static card with no event triggers — the "card pops when you first mine a deposit" just-in-time tutor does not exist and is nowhere in the 5% engine-glue budget; there is no tutorial map and no TutorialLogic anywhere; and the bot (fixed-policy UnitBuilder/BaseBuilder/Squad modules, zero diplomacy/research/convoy awareness) CANNOT play any of the four headline systems. Since OpenRA's shipped single-player IS skirmish-vs-bot, the diplomacy system — justified explicitly by "makes the strategic layer live even in skirmish-vs-AI" — degrades to the human collecting uncontested minors against a timer-bot that masses a fixed army and A-moves: the exact shallow loop the design claims to kill, now with more UI the bot ignores. The "no-dominant-strategy playtest gate" will return FALSE POSITIVES against this bot, and art money would be committed on a fun signal that was an AI artifact.

(3) The balance and scope lenses agree the asymmetry surface is mis-counted: it is not 12 matchups but 12 factions x 4 irreversible doctrines x era forks x diplomacy-on/off — hundreds of archetypes, ~4x StarCraft's surface, for a solo/tiny team. The doctrine fork the design adds to EXPRESS identity is simultaneously the largest MULTIPLIER on the matrix it must keep non-degenerate. And the on/off diplomacy toggle forks the game into two products needing two independent balance passes, with several faction identities structurally mode-dependent.

The design is unusually self-aware — it names the art ceiling, the scope risk, the determinism tax, and lists eight honest open questions. But self-awareness in prose is not scope control: it diagnoses every problem and then proposes to ship all of it anyway, just "phased." The verdict is GO on the proven nucleus, NO-GO on shipping the document. The fun is genuine and reachable in days, not years — if we serialize hard and let art throughput plus a determinism spike set the master schedule.
mustFixBeforeBuilding: NAME AND SHIP THE ZERO-ART SLICE FIRST, AS A KILL-GATE NOT A PHASE. Slice 0 = stock RA mod + ONE mechanic: capturable territory sectors that pay income, REPLACING (not augmenting) the harvester. No new factions, no diplomacy, no research, no stockpiles, no art. One question: does holding-and-cutting ground feel better than mass-and-A-move? Instrument it with a NEW first-class pacing metric the design lacks — 'camera/cursor time on your own army during contested fights.' If that single change isn't fun with reskinned RA units, the entire thesis is dead and you've spent days. Every later system is conditional on this passing.

SERIALIZE THE SYSTEMS; FORBID PARALLEL DEVELOPMENT. Cross-coupling (the design's headline virtue) is a DEVELOPMENT LIABILITY because coupled systems can't be balanced in isolation. Ship territory-economy alone and balance it; THEN add one strategic stockpile (art-free, gating an EXISTING RA superweapon as stand-in); THEN one doctrine fork. Live diplomacy/minors comes DEAD LAST — it is the riskiest new C# and the least core to the deathball thesis.

RUN A STANDALONE DETERMINISM SPIKE ON MUTABLE DIPLOMACY BEFORE designing any of the 7 agreements or UI. The ~250 LOC estimate is wrong: AlliedPlayersMask/EnemyPlayersMask (Player.cs) are set ONCE at init in CreateMapPlayers.SetupPlayerMasks and never mutated; making them mutable mid-match touches AutoTarget, Locomotor pathing, shroud recompute, frozen-actor layers, and cached IResolveOrder targeting — a new class of desync surface. Spike it as two AI players toggling Ally/Enemy mid-match on a timer under sync-hash/replay validation. If it can't be made desync-clean cheaply, CUT live diplomacy and keep static lobby-set relationships; the rest of the design survives.

BUILD THE JUST-IN-TIME CODEX AS REAL ENGINEERING OR STOP CALLING ONBOARDING SOLVED. Encyclopedia.cs (47 lines, repo-verified) is a static card with NO event hooks. The 'card pops the first time you mine a deposit' tutor requires new C#: notify hooks + a HintManager + a per-profile 'seen' set. Until it exists and is playtested, treat onboarding as UNSOLVED. Also: there is NO tutorial map and NO TutorialLogic in the repo — a 4X-hybrid cannot ship with zero guided first hour.

SCOPE AI AS A FIRST-CLASS DELIVERABLE PER SYSTEM, OR DEFAULT THE SYSTEM OFF IN SKIRMISH. The bot (fixed-policy modules, repo-verified) can play NONE of the four systems. Every new system must DEGRADE GRACEFULLY to a competent fixed bot policy (bid on nearest minor on a budget; tech on a counter-trigger not a pure timer; auto-allocate interceptors), OR get a per-system lobby default-off like ranked 1v1. Add the missing open question the doc never asks: 'Can the bot play, and not be exploited through, each system?'

DEMOTE DEFENSE FROM A LIVE MINIGAME TO SET-AND-FORGET-WITH-ONE-INTERRUPT. Keep the cost-exchange/saturation idea (genuinely good) but resolve interception AUTOMATICALLY via pre-set target-priority toggles and auto-fired magazines. Give the defender exactly ONE optional active verb per assault, not 2-4. The strategic decision lives BEFORE the fight (provisioning/positioning), preserving twitch attention for the attack. This also makes defense AI-playable.

PICK ONE PRIMARY CUSTOMER AND BALANCE FOR IT. Diplomacy-off ranked 1v1 and the rich FFA/skirmish hybrid are two different games. Make lean ranked 1v1 (3-4 factions, one stockpile, no irreversible fork, diplomacy off) the BALANCE-PRIMARY shipping product; sell the 12-bloc/diplomacy/minors vision as an explicitly-not-esports rich mode. Stop trying to make one ruleset serve both.

DEFAULT TO FLAVOR-NEUTRAL FICTIONAL BLOCS as the primary art/string set, real-country flavor as an optional skin. Removes content-policy/storefront risk and halves worst-case Codex/localization duplication (one canonical naming set).
roadmap.verticalSlice: TWO-STAGE vertical slice. STAGE 0 (zero art, days of work, the real proof-of-thesis): the stock RA mod with ONE change — the map is divided into capturable territory sectors that generate Credits; capturing replaces the harvester loop, and sectors connect to your base through cuttable supply lines. Reskinned existing RA units only. The ONLY question: does holding-and-cutting ground beat mass-and-A-move? Gate with 'camera-time-on-own-army-during-fights.' If this fails, stop. STAGE 1 (the first PLAYABLE contemporary slice, gated on Stage 0 passing): exactly 3 flavor-neutral blocs spanning the design space — one elite-expensive (USA-flavored 'Federation'), one cheap-swarm (Iran/Turkey-flavored 'Coalition'), one defensive-denial (Israel/China-flavored 'Shield Bloc'). These differ ONLY in YAML stats + a palette/skin swap on a SHARED base set initially — NO bespoke hero sprites until balance is proven. Systems present: territory-economy + exactly ONE strategic stockpile (Rare Earths gating a drone/EW doctrine via an existing RA superweapon stand-in). NO live diplomacy, NO research tree, NO minors, NO food/water meter in this slice. ~8-10 shared base units + ~6 buildings. Ship it beside classic RA via the runtime toggle. Prove a NEWCOMER can have fun AND explain why they lost (add a post-match loss-reason line) before adding layer two. This is the design's own MVP instinct enforced as a hard gate rather than an aspiration — and it is the deliverable that converts 'is this fun' from faith to evidence.

roadmap.artPipelinePlan:
HYBRID PIPELINE, PROOF-OF-CONCEPT FIRST, with a hard split by rotational requirement. The governing rule (from the C&C Remaster postmortem): at fixed top-down RTS zoom, MORE realism reads WORSE — target clean-and-bold, silhouette-first, every unit ID-able as a flat black silhouette at 100% zoom.

THE SPLIT (non-negotiable): (A) IN-WORLD ROTATING UNIT BODIES (the 32-facing sprites) go through BLENDER 3D-TURNTABLE ONLY. AI image generation is structurally BAD at rotational consistency — silhouette flips and palette drift across angles are its documented #1 failure mode — so it is FORBIDDEN for the rotation set. Pipeline: Blender model -> orthographic turntable render at 360/32 = 11.25deg steps at OpenRA's classic ~30-35deg camera pitch -> downscale -> indexed palette -> a SEPARATE remap-mask pass quantized onto OpenRA's reserved PlayerColorRemap indices. Team color is designed in from frame one as a flat unlit remap ramp (beauty pass + mask pass), NOT painted later. This is exactly how Westwood and the Remaster did it and gives rotationally-perfect facings by construction. (B) EVERYTHING SINGLE-ANGLE goes through GPT-IMAGE — this is where AI excels: concept/silhouette exploration, sidebar build-icon cameos, faction iconography, loading/menu/hero art, and especially the Codex hero plates.

PROOF-OF-CONCEPT-FIRST (the de-risk): Before committing to ANY roster, push exactly ONE unit fully end-to-end — Blender -> 32 facings -> downscale -> index -> team-color remap -> in-engine -> readability sign-off at REAL combat zoom — and MEASURE the wall-clock. Multiply by the honest base-set count (~150-250 sequences for a contemporary military set, because nothing in RA/CnC reads as modern) to get a truthful timeline. If one artist can't sustain that throughput, the project is multi-year by arithmetic; decide that deliberately. The engine plumbing already exists (RenderVoxels lighting params, PngSheetLoader RGBA path, PlayerColorRemap, the TiberianDawnHD runtime classic/HD toggle proving asset-toggling) — this is an ASSET effort, not an engine rewrite. The 'revamp' layer (soft drop shadows, base-contact AO, restrained bloom, gentle depth cue) is engine-side shader work that upgrades ALL existing art at once BEFORE a single new unit is drawn — ship that first so the retro-but-revamped look is provable on free assets. Roll out by COMPLETE faction+terrain sets (never mixed-asset), shipped beside classic via the runtime toggle, with readability sign-off at combat zoom as a hard gate before scaling. Scope discipline: one shared modern base set reused by all blocs via palette/skin swap; each faction gets ONLY its one signature unit + one signature building as bespoke art — and only after that faction is proven fun in YAML-only form.
roadmap.detail:
DECISION IN ONE LINE: GO build the territory-is-economy nucleus on a flavor-neutral contemporary reskin; NO-GO on shipping the 12-bloc / 4-system / live-diplomacy document as written. The fun is real and the panel unanimously locates it in ONE mechanic; the rest is ambition writing checks the production reality cannot cash.

WHY I DID NOT SIMPLY AVERAGE THE PANEL: the lenses cluster, and the clustering is the finding. The two 'risky' verdicts (cognitive-load, single-player/AI) and the three 'fun-with-fixes' verdicts (pacing, balance, scope) all point at the SAME structural fault from different angles: the design puts strategic decisions on the OPPONENT's tempo and INSIDE fights, leans on onboarding/AI safety nets that are repo-verified vaporware, and mis-counts a combinatorial balance surface no small team can tame. When five independent critics converge on one fault, that fault is load-bearing, not stylistic. So the honest synthesis is not '3.5/5, ship with tweaks' — it is 'the nucleus is a GO and everything else is gated behind proving the nucleus.'

WHAT I VERIFIED IN-REPO (the panel's most damaging claims are TRUE): Encyclopedia.cs is 47 lines — a static card with no event triggers, so the 'just-in-time tutor that pops when you mine a deposit' does not exist. There is NO tutorial map under mods/ra/maps and NO TutorialLogic in Widgets/Logic — the engine has never taught anyone anything. The bot is fixed-policy (BaseBuilder/UnitBuilder/Squad/SupportPower modules) with zero diplomacy/research/convoy/era awareness, so it cannot PLAY any of the four headline systems. Conversely the SYSTEMS feasibility holds: ProductionQueue (813 LOC) is a real ResearchQueue template, PlayerResources (264) is cleanly cloneable, JamsMissiles is a real PointDefense seed. So the panel's asymmetry is correct: the engine is cheap, which means ALL project risk collapses onto BALANCE, CONTENT, ART, ONBOARDING, and AI — exactly the five things the design is most optimistic and least concrete about.

WHAT SURVIVES AND MUST BE PROTECTED: territory-is-economy (every lens loves it), the era-gate spine (4 tiers, bounded snowball), saturation-vulnerable defense as a CONCEPT (its live-micro DELIVERY is the only problem), the minor-faction race (the best original idea — but the most art-blocked and the thing the bot can't contest), and the metric-gated playtest discipline. The honest forecast of what gets CUT under reality: live diplomacy + minors (riskiest C#, least core), blocs 7-12 (never balanced), 2 of 3 stockpiles, the layered-AD ladder collapsing to 1-2 tiers, the UI overhaul shrinking to 'keep the sidebar, add counters,' and bespoke art for 3-4 factions at most. If the team plans for THAT endgame deliberately, it is a shippable, genuinely novel, fun OpenRA mod in a realistic timeframe. If it tries to ship the document, the failure mode is the one the doc itself names: unfinished design, not bad design.

THE ONE RULE THAT MAKES IT FUN: push every strategic system toward 'set it between fights, it runs itself during fights, it generates at most one DEFERRABLE alert,' and keep the tactical fight as autopilot-light on defense as RA's is. Re-anchor on Rise of Nations correctly — strategic layer = low-frequency background state, tactical layer = the clean twitch fight. Prove that on Phase 0 with the new camera-time metric before adding a single further layer, and 'fast Stellaris' stops being an assertion and becomes a measured property. Ship broad before proving it, and the battlefield the user loves quietly loses to the dashboard the design admires.
